Sports.title: Some of the elites criticising Gianni Infantino are sheer hypocrites. How can the money-obsessed leeches behind the Super League expect us to listen to their confected moral outrage as they bleed our beloved game dry, writes IAN HERBERT
Sports.content:
The most preposterous man in football is staggering on, drowning in such vanity and ego that he cannot see how he embarrasses himself, so perhaps that’s why the biggest hypocrites of another dark week for football appear to have got away with it.

On Sunday, Real Madrid decided to weigh in on the Gianni Infantino scandal, instructing their media people to put out a sanctimonious statement welcoming the scrapping of the egghead’s plans to sell off a slice of the World Cup, and thanking UEFA for fulfilling their ‘duty’ to ‘protect football’.

You really could not make some of this stuff up. Yes, that moralising really did come from the same Real Madrid whose avarice stank football out when they led the contemptible group of 12 clubs who attempted the European Super League breakaway coup, a few years back.

Infantino’s intellectual and moral decrepitude may have been there for us all to see in his email offering nations a small cash consideration if they back his plans to raise $20billion, but have we forgotten the European club men with whiteboards and coloured marker pens, explaining their own despicable little earner in 2021?

Real’s executives back then were just as atrocious as Infantino is now – worse, in fact, given that the FIFA scheme was not actually a breakaway proposal designed to leave the have-nots behind – while the money men they indirectly inveighed against on Sunday are the one and the same suits from JPMorgan Chase, hired by them to advise on the Super League.

Given that the US finance house were forced to apologise for their part in that episode, you might have fancied they’d learned their lesson about how ferocious the backlash to a sell-out like this would be. No. They just couldn’t resist getting their snouts in the football trough again.

Gianni Infantino is somehow staggering on as FIFA President, drowning in such vanity and ego that he cannot see how he embarrasses himself

But many of his critics do not have a leg to stand on. These are clubs that tried to form the breakaway European Super League - and only buckled after immense fan pressure (pictured)

So, please let’s get this right. The new flank in football's civil war is not between the idealists and the profiteers, but between competing profiteers fighting over who gets to cash in on the game.

UEFA, under Aleksander Ceferin, are currently casting themselves as the defenders of football's traditions, protectors of the meritocracy, guardians of the fans against billionaire opportunists. Yet this is the self-same organisation which expanded the Champions League into a sprawling competition with 64 extra fixtures in 2024, to create greater TV income and more sponsorship revenue.

The self-same organisation which has been engaged in a pitched battle for territory with FIFA. That fight has spawned the Nations League and the expanded Club World Cup, with each governing body viewing the other’s new tournament with deep suspicion. UEFA’s objection is not to football becoming more commercial but to someone else collecting the commercial rewards.

Our own Premier League claim a moral high ground for themselves, too, proclaiming to be the world's greatest and most unpredictable domestic competition, while generating more money than any such league in history. Yet it is driven by the same monopolistic greed, behaving as though sharing a fraction of the wealth with the rest of the football pyramid would be an act of unconscionable sacrifice.

Don’t let it be forgotten that its biggest clubs, led by Liverpool and Manchester United, made their own power grab through Project Big Picture in 2020. Or that the Premier League held talks with CVC Capital Partners, one of the world's largest private equity firms, about selling a stake in future broadcasting and commercial revenues, at the same time.

That came to nothing, either, but here was an elite equally willing to explore new ways of extracting financial value from our game. The people’s game.

Whenever the redistribution of Premier League wealth is discussed, we witness the language and narrative suddenly change and those overseeing the competition which has negotiated television contracts worth billions begin to fret about the pennies.

It was clear when a White Paper on football governance was published a few years back that a greater flow of money down from the Premier League would be egregiously hard to extract.

UEFA, under Aleksander Ceferin (right), are casting themselves as the defenders of football's traditions. Yet they expanded and distorted the Champions League to generate more revenue

It shouldn't be forgotten that the Premier League's biggest clubs, led by Liverpool and Manchester United, made their own power grab through Project Big Picture in 2020

The gilded elite division continued to maintain the fallacy that they were helping the rest, when 70 per cent of the money they sent down below was Championship parachute money. An insurance policy for the division’s own members laughably dressed up as ‘solidarity payments’.

It has taken Government intervention to force a more equitable share of the Premier League’s wealth throughout the game, in the shape of the Independent Football Regulator, with its ‘backstop’ power to force a settlement if none is agreed.

Faced with such a prospect, the Premier League have finally just voted for an additional £1.5billion from those in the gilded cage, to be shared with the EFL’s clubs, though even that is not allocated yet. The cash, to be funded by a two per cent lift in the transfer levy on all top-flight deals, will clearly need to be crowbarred from clubs swimming in wealth, given the opposition led by Manchester City’s petro-dollar billionaire owners – another of the merry little European Super League band.

We understand other members of the so-called ‘Big Six’ are also unhappy that they may now find themselves coughing up more than less elevated Premier League clubs. It’s been left to the more moderately wealthy members of the division, who faced down the big clubs over the Super League, to challenge them again.

If there was one positive to come out of the Super League scandal, it was the way it cut the grasping, spiritually remote 'Big Six' down to size. 'It's like emerging from a slightly abusive relationship,' the owner of one of the smaller Premier League clubs told me at the time.

This weekend, the FA Cup begins its beautiful seasonal arc once more, carrying the customary thrill and sense of pride among all who will compete in its extra preliminary round. North Ferriby, at home to St Helens, Northwich Victoria, playing away to Beverley Town, and Nelson, entertaining Stockport Georgians, are just three of those taking part who know what a precarious financial reality and existential threat look and feel like.

For all the weekend’s 438 competing clubs, reaching the first round proper – six ties away, in November – would be monumental, with £47,750 prize money for those who win at that stage.

But any who progress that far will also experience the chill of strictures forced down from the top of the game. This will be the second season with no replays from the first round proper onwards – a diminishment the FA said was necessary because of increasing pressure on the calendar, particularly following UEFA's expansion of their club competitions.

The early rounds of the FA Cup still bring with them a sense of thrill and pride - though replays with England's top clubs are now sadly a thing of the past

Infantino is taking the logic of those presiding over the elite game to its natural conclusion, not dragging them somewhere they do not wish to go

Critics, especially in the EFL and non-League, have argued that a vital source of income is being removed from smaller clubs, who can no longer earn lucrative replay gates against bigger opponents.

But those little people are shouting in the dark. The abolition of replays, fourth-round matches spread over five days and the scheduling of the 2027 final before the Premier League campaign finishes, rather than as the climax to the season, belong to the story of the competition’s devaluation and diminishment. The Cup has been crushed into virtual irrelevance by football's high and mighty.

As of last night, Infantino’s brazen conceit and vanity were keeping him in a job which any intelligent and self-respecting industry would by now have forced him from. He is no doubt banking on the relentless news cycle moving on and UEFA’s threat to boycott FIFA’s competition receding into the distance.

Qualification games for the 2030 World Cup are just a year away and Infantino can safely calculate that national associations will not want to take the financial hit that a boycott would carry. It seems significant, and concerning, that a mere 11 national associations, including England and Wales, have voiced opposition to him remaining in post.

Yet for all the sound and fury, there is something deeply unsettling and incomplete about some of this moralising. Infantino is taking the logic of those presiding over the elite game to its natural conclusion, not dragging them somewhere they do not wish to go. He is the most despicable emblem of a game which is slowly devouring itself, but by no means the only one.

Sports.title: Inside Sir Ben Ainslie's mission to finally end Britain's wait for America's Cup glory: How history - and a secret weapon - are inspiring Olympic legend's team in Naples
Sports.content:
A couple of notable letters crop up on the wall. They are correspondence from Lord Nelson and nestle among the high-value art in the Royal Yacht Squadron ‘Castle’, in Cowes, Isle of Wight.

The handwriting looked fine to me, a nice round hand.

Said James, steward of the place, where he has worked, other than for a brief spell elsewhere, since he was 16, with a degree of understatement: ‘There is a reason it is not quite as legible as it might have been.

‘By this stage, the Admiral was no longer able to write with his stronger arm.’

So, we are at the very citadel of sailing, a place built with eight-feet deeper walls on the land side than on the waterfront. ‘The French would have known better than to have approached us by sea,’ was the thrust of James’s non-negotiable reasoning.

He was wearing a black tie. All staff and some 540 members of the Royal Yacht Squadron wear the same neckwear along with their dark blazers. They are in mourning.

Sir Ben Ainslie is looking to help end Britain's long wait for America's Cup glory

For it is merely 200 years since Admiral Nelson left us, aged 47, aboard Britain’s flagship HMS Victory, shot by a French sniper during the Battle of Trafalgar off the coast of Spain. Dead but victorious.

Which sort of brings us to today, and Sir Ben Ainslie’s attempt, now as team boss rather than helmsman, to win the technology-led, F1-on-water America’s Cup, the oldest international sports competition in the world dating back to 1851, when it is next held in Naples next year. We have famously never won it.

Ainslie was made an honorary member of the Squadron (you can’t apply, chaps or chapesses), under whose banner the British attempt fights, soon after winning his fourth Olympic Gold medal at London 2012, before being elevated to full membership three years ago.

There is a major departure in his latest attempt, however, in the male-dominated Royal Yacht Squadron. Jemima Lines, 29, a kitefoiler and adventurer, is enlisted to become a participating member of the on-board team of five, and thus the first woman to participate in the Cup since aviation pioneer Sir Thomas Sopwith’s wife Phyllis in 1934 and 1937.

Lines was given the role for her exceptional background, one entirely in keeping with the traditions of the event. For one thing, she is the fourth daughter of a special forces soldier, born in Kent and educated at Bristol University as an engineer. Her father was Ralph Crathorne, who died earlier this year, aged 67, in a mountaineering accident in Scotland.

‘I owe so much to him and how I see everything in life,’ she said during Cowes Week, only a few weeks after getting married. ‘Everything I have achieved is down to his influence. He wanted us to explore everything in the world, and I am pleased to be doing this as a result.

‘We’d often be late for school because my father had taken us all to the beach and we’d be kiting, that was from the age of eight, and he always wanted us to do bigger adventures. This is the biggest change I have ever made, to be involved in the America’s Cup.’

Ainslie, as ever, had a busy week in Cowes, being his sport’s most celebrated figure. A day earlier he had welcomed Anne, Princess Royal, as the new Admiral of the Yacht Squadron, in succession to her father, the late Duke of Edinburgh. She is a loyal supporter of the old cause.

Ainslie's wife Georgie (left) is his stalwart supporter in his ambition, now as team boss

Ainslie is now sipping a restorative drink and eating sandwiches on the Royal Yacht Squadron terrace after sailing competitively for the first time since the last America’s Cup in Barcelona a couple of years ago. He is doing his best to pretend it is not the case, but his 49-year-old body has been given a decent examination out on the water.

He is off next to the annual Squadron Ball later, along with wife Georgie (née Thompson), previously of Sky Sports News, his stalwart supporter.

Sitting close to where the America’s Cup began under the gaze of Queen Victoria, Ainslie said: ‘I’m confident we can win the Cup in the end. You know how it is with our maritime history. We have to do it.’

Handwriting, good, bad or indifferent, it is a story that would earn its place on the Castle wall.

Sports.title: What happened to the last West Ham starting XI that were embarrassed in Carabao Cup round one
Sports.content:
What happened to the last West Ham starting XI that were embarrassed in Carabao Cup round one

West Ham are set to play a League Cup first round match for the first time in more than a decade

View 5 Images Sam Allardyce's West Ham were stunned in the League Cup in 2011 (Image: Nicky Hayes/Shutterstock)

West Ham's relegation from the Premier League has brought plenty of upheaval and not just in terms of squad ins and outs. It also means the Hammers will play in the opening round of the Carabao Cup for the first time in more than a decade.

‌



Nuno Espirito Santo's team face Portsmouth this weekend before beginning their Championship campaign eight days later. It is their first time entering the League Cup at this stage since they were last in the second tier, back in 2011.

‌



In fact, so much time has passed since then that it was called the Carling Cup rather than the Carabao Cup when West Ham hosted Aldershot in August 2011. The match was played at Upton Park, the ground the London side left in 2016.

‌



Sam Allardyce was in the dugout for the Aldershot match, with his team falling to a shock 2-1 defeat against the League Two side. Here, we've taken a look at the players who turned out for the Hammers that night.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Carabao Cup draw confirmed as final fixtures announced for round one READ MORE :

Ruud Boffin

Belgian goalkeeper Boffin played just three times for West Ham. The first came in the Premier League, on a snowy day against Blackburn and the last came against Sheffield Wednesday in the 2011/12 FA Cup, a few months after his Aldershot start.

‌



He left West Ham in the summer of 2012 and spent the following decade in Turkey, racking up a century of appearances for both Eskisehirspor and Antalyaspor before retiring in 2022. He scored his only career goal for the former when a free-kick from deep inside his own half flew into the opposition net without bouncing.

Julien Faubert

Faubert was known among fans of other clubs for his unexpected loan stint at Real Madrid but the France international's best West Ham form came after he returned from that stint. Having played as a winger early in his career, he was used as a full-back under Allardyce and predecessor Avram Grant.

View 5 Images Julien Faubert stayed to help West Ham win promotion (Image: Richard Heathcote/Getty Images)

‌

Learn more £44 Sky Get the deal here Product Description Sky's Ultimate TV and Sky Sports bundle includes at least 215 live Premier League clashes across the 2026/27 season with more than 1,400 live games across the EFL and beyond, plus F1, golf and darts. Every subscription now comes with 135 channels alongside free subscriptions to HBO Max, Netflix, Disney+, discovery+ and Hayu.

The 2012 play-off final would be his last Hammers game, after which he travelled the world. He had spells in Turkey, France, Scotland, Finland and Borneo - also playing international football for Martinique after switching his FIFA nationality - before retiring in 2020.

Winston Reid

Reid was one of the relegated stars who stayed and helped West Ham return to the Premier League. The New Zealander went on to captain the team and became a fan favourite, even scoring the last ever league goal at Upton Park.

‌



He was blighted by injuries in the latter part of his Hammers career and had loan spells with Sporting Kansas City and Brentford, playing his final club match in 2021. The centre-back was also handed an international farewell the following year, captaining the All Whites against Australia before hanging up his boots.

Callum McNaughton

Homegrown centre-back McNaughton was making his debut against Aldershot but it ended up in a nightmare. After being caught in possession inside his own half, he committed a last-man foul on Danny Hylton and was shown a straight red card.

View 5 Images Callum McNaughton (centre) was sent off on his debut (Image: Graham Chadwick/ANL/Shutterstock)

‌



McNaughton was loaned to AFC Wimbledon the following month and joined the League Two side permanently in January 2012. He spent most of his career in non-league football before heading to the United States for a career in teaching and football coaching,

George McCartney

Northern Ireland international McCartney was in his second Hammers spell, rejoining on loan from Sunderland as one of Allardyce's first signings. He would go on to sign permanently after promotion and finished his career at Upton Park.

Now 45 years old, he has dipped his toe into coaching. He has spent the last few years with Linfield in his home country, working as an assistant to former international team-mate David Healy.

‌



Pablo Barrera

Barrera joined West Ham after impressing for Mexico at the 2010 World Cup but underwhelmed during the relegation campaign. He would end up leaving on loan just days after the Aldershot game, spending the season in Spain with Real Zaragoza.

He would return to Mexico after that year in La Liga, playing more than 300 Liga MX games before retiring in 2025. The 39-year-old finished his career at Queretaro, with whom he racked up a century of league appearances.

Junior Stanislas

View 5 Images Stanislas scored West Ham's goal (Image: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images)

‌



Academy graduate Stanislas scored West Ham's goal against Aldershot after good pressure from Barrera forced a mistake. However, both men would be gone within a week of the defeat, with the England Under-21 international completing a permanent move to Burnley.

Eddie Howe, the manager who brought him to Turf Moor, would later engineer another reunion at Bournemouth. Stanislas spent the best part of a decade on the south coast before retiring in 2023 and has since moved into coaching, most recently working under Kieran McKenna at Ipswich.

Kevin Nolan

Nolan arrived as a marquee signing, taking the captain's armband after Matt Upson's departure. The former Newcastle and Bolton man linked up well with Allardyce again, helping clinch promotion before top scoring for the Hammers in the 2012/13 Premier League.

‌



He moved into management after leaving East London in 2015, with spells at Leyton Orient (as player-manager) and Notts County. After returning to West Ham as part of David Moyes' coaching staff, he spent time in the England youth set-up before a spell in charge of Northampton Town which ended in March this year.

Freddie Sears

Academy graduate Sears burst onto the scene as a teenage striker but was used more as a wide forward as his career progressed. He played 10 Championship games under Allardyce but joined Colchester on loan before the end of the season and later moved there permanently.

It was at Ipswich where the Essex-born talent established himself, playing more than 200 league games for the Tractor Boys. Now 36, he has returned to his roots as a goal-getter after dropping down to non-league, with his 29 league goals for Maldon & Tiptree last term making him the top scorer in the Isthmian League North.

‌



Frederic Piquionne

View 5 Images Frederic Piquionne briefly spent time on the coaching staff at Everton women (Image: Charlotte Tattersall - The FA/The FA via Getty Images)

Piquionne followed former manager Grant from Portsmouth to West Ham and ultimately suffered a second successive Premier League relegation. The striker, who won international caps for both France and Martinique, scored twice in the first half of the Championship season before making a loan switch to Doncaster Rovers.

The 47-year-old rounded off his career with spells in the United States, France and India before moving into coaching. He had a brief stint as assistant manager at Everton women when compatriot Jean-Luc Vasseur was in the dugout.

Article continues below

John Carew

Norwegian striker Carew was making his first Hammers start against Aldershot and would end the season with two league goals. He left at the end of the season and retired a little over a year later after failing to find a new club.

Since quitting football, the former Valencia star has embarked on a career change. He is now a professional actor, featuring in a number of Norwegian and English-language productions including Netflix series Home for Christmas.

Sports.title: Liverpool star refused to go on pre-season tour with £49m transfer forced through
Sports.content:
Liverpool star refused to go on pre-season tour with £49m transfer forced through

Liverpool had to contend with a key star refusing to go on a pre-season tour before forcing a transfer

View 2 Images Raheem Sterling enjoyed three formative years at Liverpool (Image: Getty)

Andoni Iraola will be grateful for the drama-less pre-season he's had with Liverpool this summer. The same couldn't be said for ex-Reds boss Brendan Rodgers, who had to contend with Raheem Sterling's refusal to go on the club's pre-season tour in July 2015.

‌



The former England star was a top target for Manchester City and in order to push through a move to the Citizens, a then-20-year-old Sterling told Rodgers that he didn't want to go on the tour to the Far East and Australia.

‌



Sterling doubled down on his desire to depart Merseyside by calling in sick to miss two days of pre-season training. A breakdown in relations between Sterling and Liverpool occurred in the 2014/15 campaign that resulted in the forward rejecting the club's offer of a new £100,000-a-week contract.

‌



The summer began with the Reds swiftly turning down two bids from City. Sterling eventually got his wish as he secured a £49m move to the Etihad Stadium later that summer.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

He ended up travelling with City to their pre-season tour of Australia and admitted he regretted the manner of his departure from Liverpool. He said at the time: "I was a bit disappointed how I left.

‌



4 transfers Liverpool need to complete after Leeds defeat showed harsh reality READ MORE :

"That was the main problem I've had with the situation - how I've left it with Liverpool. I'm good with everyone at the football club, the manager, the players and I wish them well for the new season.

"But it was really disappointing how it did finish off." However, Sterling insisted the move was the right decision for his career. He explained: "From the first moment I heard City were interested in me [I wanted to join], purely because of the direction the football club is going in.

View 2 Images The 31-year-old played a pivotal role in City's dominance under Pep Guardiola (Image: 2022 Manchester City FC)

‌



"I've met all my team-mates now and it's been a really good few days, they've made me feel welcome and I'm really happy to be here. I think I made the right decision." The 31-year-old ended up enjoying a stellar seven-year career in Manchester, winning four Premier League titles, five League Cups and one FA Cup.

Sterling ended his City career with 131 goals in 339 games and secured his legacy as one of the greatest players in the club's history. He left for Chelsea in 2022 in a £50m deal and scored 19 goals in 81 games before joining Arsenal on loan in the 2024/25 campaign.

He scored just one goal in 28 games before returning to Chelsea and mutually agreed with the club to terminate his contract. He then signed for Feyenoord in February earlier this year until the end of the season, but played in just eight games while going without a goal. Currently without a club, his future remains uncertain.

Sports.title: Liverpool news: Fresh Bradley Barcola transfer update as dressing room view on Konsa emerges
Sports.content:
Liverpool news: Fresh Bradley Barcola transfer update as dressing room view on Konsa emerges

Liverpool have received updates on multiple transfer fronts as Andoni Iraola looks to add to his summer business

View 2 Images Liverpool have received a concerning update regarding their pursuit of PSG's Bradley Barcola (Image: FRANCK FIFE, AFP via Getty Images)

Liverpool are running out of time to wrap up the business required to put them back in contention for Premier League honours this season. The Reds have already overhauled their coaching staff after Andoni Iraola replaced Arne Slot at the helm but the general consensus is that the Reds require more reinforcements.

‌



Weeks have passed since Jeremy Jacquet and Victor Munoz were confirmed as Liverpool's first signings of the summer.

‌



A top-tier replacement for Mohamed Salah remains a pressing concern for the club entering an important stage of the transfer calendar. Mirror Football provides a breakdown of the latest transfer speculation around Anfield this weekend.

‌



FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Arsenal enter Barcola race

Liverpool's pursuit of Bradley Barcola could become more complicated after Arsenal reportedly entered the race for his services. And it leaves the Reds at further risk of frustration after Real Madrid beat them to the signing of Yan Diomande.

Why Yan Diomande decided against Liverpool transfer after meeting Andoni Iraola READ MORE :

Barcola was tipped as Liverpool's back-up option, with talks reportedly underway to get a deal done. However, Arsenal have also been stumped by Real after Vinicius Jr allegedly considered a move to the Emirates before penning a contract extension.

‌



That's led them to pivot their interests in the search for a left winger, with Barcola seemingly their next top choice. Mikel Arteta has already brought in Christos Tzolis as a replacement for Leandro Trossard but he wants more competition for the role.

The Independent reported Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez and Everton forward Iliman Ndiaye are also being monitored by Arsenal. Alvarez has indicated he'd like to leave Los Rojiblancos but Diego Simeone doesn't want to sell.

Find out more here.

‌



That could steer the north Londoners further in Barcola's direction, which won't be welcome news at Anfield. The current Premier League champions are one of the few teams in England that may boast greater appeal than Liverpool in the current market.

The Reds have reportedly agreed personal terms with Barcola and are searching to find an agreement with PSG. The Parisiens were demanding as much as £145million for their player, though a more manageable figure of £109m has since emerged.

Dressing room view on Konsa transfer

View 2 Images Aston Villa players are reportedly 'increasingly concerned' Ezri Konsa will leave the club this summer (Image: Neville Williams/Aston Villa FC via Getty Images)

‌



The Aston Villa squad are reported to be 'increasingly concerned' Ezri Konsa will leave this summer. That's according to the Daily Mail, which has suggested Liverpool target Konsa is edging closer to a move.

Despite already adding Jeremy Jacquet to their ranks this summer, more defensive reinforcements are believed to remain a priority at Anfield. That has perhaps been exacerbated by Joe Gomez's recent injury setback, while Jacquet and fellow youngster Giovanni Leoni are still regaining full fitness following injuries.

A major sticking point in Konsa's case would be Villa's supposed £60million valuation. That figure would be hefty for most centre-backs but particularly one who's set to turn 29 in October and has less than two years left on his contract.

Article continues below

It's frustrating for Liverpool, therefore, that Konsa could fit their requirements so succinctly. The England star can play at centre-back or right-back, the same two areas in which Liverpool's defence is most in need of reinforcements.

Sports.title: Arsenal news: £73m Man Utd transfer target eyed as club 'resigned to losing' key player
Sports.content:
Arsenal news: £73m Man Utd transfer target eyed as club 'resigned to losing' key player

Arsenal appear to be pushing on with their summer transfer business after losing the chance to sign Vinicius Jr from Real Madrid

View 3 Images Mikel Arteta is eyeing up more potential Arsenal incomings (Image: Getty)

Arsenal have supposedly set their sights on another attacking player after failing to land Vinicius Jr. The Gunners will be out to defend their Premier League crown with the new season approaching.

‌



Mikel Arteta's side are still in the market for a forward this summer with pre-season in full flow. The manager was extremely interested in bringing Vinicius Jr to the Premier League after his contract negotiations with Real Madrid stalled. However, the Brazilian winger has now secured a new deal until 2032, putting to bed the chance of an exit.

‌



Now, the reigning Premier League champions will reportedly move on to other targets, including a £ 73 million-rated striker who Manchester United are also eyeing. Here, Mirror Football has the latest coming out of the red side of north London.

‌



FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Vinicius Jr to Arsenal transfer saga reaches conclusion as Real Madrid star strikes agreement READ MORE :

£73m Man Utd transfer target eyed

After failing to sign Vinicius Jr, Arsenal may end up competing with United for the signature of Inter Milan's Pio Esposito. The Sun reports that the Gunners sent scouts to Inter's pre-season derby against AC Milan to keep tabs on the 21-year-old.

View 3 Images Esposito has reportedly emerged as a target for the Gunners (Image: Getty)

‌



It is claimed that Arteta is planning to add to his striking department, which includes Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz, and the 6ft3in Esposito has impressed him in recent months. United are also thought to be keen on the young striker but, unlike Arsenal, are not planning to rush into an offer.

However, Inter have publicly stated that Esposito is "untouchable" to try and ward off European clubs. But it's reported that the Serie A outfit has placed a £73m price tag in private, in case offers do come rolling in.

Sources close to Esposito claim that, whilst he is committed to Inter, the allure of the Premier League is on his mind. He is understood to be open to a move to England.

‌



Aston Villa 'resigned to losing' key player

Elsewhere, Aston Villa are reportedly 'resigned to losing' Ezri Konsa as Arsenal stump up their offer for the veteran defender. Arteta raised interest in the centre-half after losing William Saliba to a back injury at the World Cup, and now is handling injuries to Ben White and Jurrien Timber.

View 3 Images Konsa could soon be heading to north London (Image: Getty)

‌



The 28-year-old is a primary target for the Gunners but their initial bid was understood to be just over half of Villa's £60m price tag. However, the The Mail reports that Villa are growing "increasingly concerned" that Konsa could be off this summer.

Konsa's own team-mates are reportedly worried that he is planning an exit, with Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans having already departed this summer. Liverpool are also handling a defensive crisis of their own and could swoop in for Konsa.

Virgil van Dijk is now returning to the squad post-World Cup, but with a pre-season injury to Joe Gomez and an absence of Jeremy Jacquet in other friendly fixtures, Andoni Iraola's side needs reinforcements quickly.

Sports.title: Gabriel Jesus' agent addresses Arsenal transfer exit after being spotted at rival club
Sports.content:
Gabriel Jesus' agent addresses Arsenal transfer exit after being spotted at rival club

Gabriel Jesus has been made available for a transfer by Arsenal this summer and his agent has now been spotted at the training ground of Napoli amid reported negotiations

View 2 Images Gabriel Jesus could leave Arsenal this summer (Image: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

Gabriel Jesus' agent has insisted that he was not at Napoli's training ground on Friday to discuss a potential transfer for the Arsenal striker. Jesus has entered the final year of his contract with Arsenal and, having fallen down the pecking order after injuries, could be let go this summer.

‌



The Gunners have Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz as their first-choice strikers and are in the market for another attacker, with Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez on the wish list after Vinicius Junior decided to stay with Real Madrid.

‌



Mikel Arteta is understood to have green lighted an exit for Jesus, who only made 14 Premier League appearances last season, as well as Gabriel Martinelli. The 29-year-old has been with Arsenal for four years and the club are keen to cash in, rather than lose him for nothing next year.

‌



Napoli are interested in signing Jesus, with Romelu Lukaku and Lorenzo Lucca potentially heading for the exit. Arsenal want a permanent transfer worth €20million (£17m), while the Italian giants are keen to negotiate that fee downwards.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Arsenal could break unwanted transfer record as Mikel Arteta green lights two deals READ MORE :

Jesus' agent Giovanni Branchini was spotted at Napoli's training ground in Castel di Sangro on Friday, heightening speculation that a deal could be close. But Branchini has insisted that he was visiting the club to see another of his clients, Napoli boss Massimiliano Allegri.

‌



“Allegri and I have been in touch, I came here today to come and visit him,” Branchini told Videoinformazioni.com. “He’s working hard and he’s happy with everything. He’s always had a good opinion of this team and is satisfied with the work that is being done.”

Quizzed on Jesus, Branchini said: “I haven’t spoken to Allegri about him.” And asked if Lukaku and Lucca would have to be sold for Jesus to join, he added: “In my line of work, the ‘ifs’ count for very little, not as much as they matter for you journalists. From my point of view, it’s better to not talk about speculation.”

View 2 Images Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus could both be sold this summer (Image: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

‌



Allegri will build his attack around Rasmus Hojlund in the 2026/27 season after the Danish striker completed a permanent £38m move from Manchester United following a successful loan spell. But there is room for another forward, with Lukaku poised to move on and Lucca facing an uncertain future too.

Arsenal have so far only managed to move on Leandro Trossard (£17m to Besiktas), Jakub Kiwior (£14.7m to Porto), Karl Hein (£2.5m to Werder Bremen) and Christian Norgaard (£7m to Everton) this summer. Arteta knows that shifting other fringe players will be key if they are to land a world-class attacker and a centre-back to provide cover for the injured William Saliba.

Jesus has struggled for consistency at Arsenal, with injuries hampering the Brazilian. He has failed to live up to his £45m fee from Manchester City in 2022 and has seen his chances of game time dramatically reduced by the arrival of Gyokeres last summer.

Sports.title: Liverpool prepare blockbuster offer for PSG star Bradley Barcola - but there's a catch
Sports.content:
Liverpool prepare blockbuster offer for PSG star Bradley Barcola - but there's a catch

Bradley Barcola is Liverpool's top transfer target this summer and the Reds are now ready to move forward with trying to sign the Paris Saint-Germain winger

View 2 Images Bradley Barcola is Liverpool's top transfer target (Image: Getty Images)

Liverpool are ready to make their opening offer for Paris Saint-Germain winger Bradley Barcola, but their bid will be rejected by the French giants.

‌



Barcola has emerged as Liverpool's number one transfer target this summer, with new manager Andoni Iraola desperate to strengthen in wide areas. The France international has entered the final two years of his current contract with PSG, who have softened their stance on a deal.

‌



The reigning Champions League champions had initially been firm in their stance that the 23-year-old was not for sale at any price. But, having lined up potential replacements, a deal can now be done - if their asking price is met.

‌



Liverpool have found it slow going in the transfer window this summer, with a £35million deal for Osasuna winger Victor Munoz the only significant piece of business done, as the £55m arrival of Jeremy Jacquet was sealed in January.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Liverpool weigh up hijacking £60m Arsenal transfer to appease desperate Andoni Iraola READ MORE :

But the Reds are now ready to step up negotiations with PSG for Barcola, according to L'Equipe. They will submit an official offer in the region of €115million (£98m) in the expectation that it will be rejected.

‌



PSG don't want to lose Barcola, who has contributed heavily to their success under Luis Enrique's management. Yet they are also unwilling to keep a player against his will, so have slapped a €150 million (£128.5m) price tag on their star player.

Their resolve has likely be strengthened by the £120m fee RB Leipzig got from Real Madrid for Yan Diomande - a player four years younger and with far less experience than Barcola.

Barcola has 39 goals in 152 appearances for the club since joining from Lyon three years ago. He has combined well with Ousmane Dembele and Desire Doue under Enrique's management, but is keen to join Liverpool.

‌



View 2 Images Andoni Iraola is desperate for a new winger (Image: Michael Miller/ISI Photos, ISI Photos via Getty Images)

Barcola has already agreed personal terms with Liverpool and it seems likely that a deal can be done. Liverpool sporting director Richard Hughes is leading discussions, with Luis Campos representing PSG and agent Moussa Sissoko speaking on behalf of Barcola.

L'Equipe says that Liverpool are not actively pursuing any alternative to Barcola, which is a measure of their determination to land the Frenchman. Iraola spoke publicly about the need for a winger, even after Munoz was signed.

‌



"There are obvious situations that we know where we need to sign players," he said last month. "A winger, for example – we definitely need to sign a winger.

"But there are other situations that we will have to analyse what the market gives you, what’s the cost, how we also see the players we have. We have some tricky positions where we have injured players that we trust but is still not the ideal situation. So, it will depend on a lot of things."

Sports.title: UEFA could boycott 5 tournaments in next 11 months after new Gianni Infantino statement
Sports.content:
UEFA could boycott 5 tournaments in next 11 months after new Gianni Infantino statement

Gianni Infantino is determined to cling onto power as FIFA president and his refusal to resign in the wake of the World Cup private investment scandal could force UEFA into action

View 2 Images Gianni Infantino is ready for the fight (Image: AP Photo/Martin Meissner)

UEFA could be forced to carry out their threat of boycotting FIFA tournaments in less than a month after Gianni Infantino refused to give in to the mounting pressure on him to resign.

‌



Rather than fall on his sword, Infantino has made moves to solidify his position as FIFA president. Following seven hours of crisis talks in Morocco on Wednesday, FIFA released a statement saying Infantino had their "full support" after his botched attempt to invite private investment into tournaments.

‌



FIFA have opted to close ranks and go on the offensive, saying they will "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation".

‌



The battle lines have been drawn, with UEFA leading the backlash against Infantino. The Football Association has followed in Wales' footsteps by formally withdrawing their support of the Swiss, but with the pressure yet to tell, UEFA and their allies may have to follow through with their threat.

Gianni Infantino state of play as 211 nations decide desperate FIFA president's fate READ MORE :

Argentina at odds with England as statement released on FIFA president Gianni Infantino READ MORE :

In a statement on Thursday, UEFA said FIFA's words following their meeting "changes nothing" and that their threat of a boycott stands. It means FIFA have been put on notice ahead of their next international tournament, the Under-20 Women's World Cup, which is scheduled to be hosted in Poland, beginning on September 5.

After that comes the Under-17 Women's World Cup in Morocco in October and the Under-17 World Cup in Qatar in November and December. Next summer comes a much bigger fish: the Women's World Cup in Brazil. If it came to it, boycotting that would send a strong message - and it is a sacrifice England star Lucy Bronze is willing to make.

‌



FIFA tournaments UEFA could boycott FIFA Under-20 Women's World Cup (Poland) - September 2026 FIFA Under-17 Women's World Cup (Morocco) - October 2026 FIFA Under-17 World Cup (Qatar) -November/December 2026 FIFA Women's Champions Cup (Miami) -January 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup (Brazil) - June/July 2027

“The message that we stand by … is ‘for the good of the game’. The players who play in those competitions, the European players, we stand by our beliefs and what the right thing is for our game,” Bronze said ahead of a Chelsea pre-season friendly in New Zealand.

“If that means boycotting competitions, then that has to happen. It’s for the future of the game and not just for me today and tomorrow, it’s for all the little girls or little boys who come after us to make sure that they’re in a good place, when the game is moving forward in decades to come, not just tomorrow.”

‌



With Infantino not willing to resign, UEFA may have to back a rival candidate in the upcoming FIFA presidential election. Infantino has been in charge for 10 years and was set to stand unopposed for a fourth term next year, but the events of the past week have changed everything.

View 2 Images UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin is leading the effort to oust Gianni Infantino (Image: Nicolò Campo/LightRocket via Getty Images)

A UEFA statement shared on Thursday afternoon read: "UEFA's associations were very clear about the conditions attached to the non-participation in FIFA competitions.

‌



"First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn, and secondly, assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again.

"These conditions have not been met. In addition, UEFA made it abundantly clear in its statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's presidency. That position holds.

"Yesterday's (Wednesday) announcement that some people employed by the FIFA President (and whose careers depend on his favour) agree with him changes nothing."

Sports.title: 'Number one priority' - Amy Hunt makes intentions clear ahead of home European Athletics Championships
Sports.content:
'Number one priority' - Amy Hunt makes intentions clear ahead of home European Athletics Championships

The sprint sensation claimed Commonwealth Games silver over 100m and is now looking to make her mark in Birmingham

View Image Amy Hunt. (Image: imagecomms/Team England)

Amy Hunt has made a promise to the fans in Birmingham this summer – they will be seeing plenty of her at the European Athletics Championships.

‌



The World Championship silver medallist over 200m has made the Europeans her absolute priority this summer and will compete over both 100m and 200m individually, as well as in two relays at the Alexander Stadium.

‌



That makes for a packed schedule, but Hunt would not have it any other way, in her first chance to compete at a major outdoor championship on home soil.

‌



She explained: “One of the great things about being a versatile sprinter is that I can compete over both the 100m and 200m. The downside is there are lots of opportunities, so sometimes it's difficult to say no.

“Our number one priority is the European Championships. It's the first time they've been held in the UK, so we're aiming to compete in the full programme there: the 100m, 200m, women's 4x100m and the new mixed 4x100m, because that would be really iconic.

“I'll be doing everything, so you'll probably be seeing a lot of me every day.”

‌



The mixed 4x100m relay will be particularly interesting, as it makes its major championships debut at the Alexander Stadium.

Hunt has shown her value as a relay runner in taking Olympic silver two years ago, a matter of weeks after a European gold, both in the women’s 4x100m.

And while sprinting is a very individual sport, Hunt relishes the opportunity to join forces with the likes of Dina Asher-Smith and Daryll Neita to bring back medals.

‌



She said: “That's one of the beautiful things about relays. Everyone brings different strengths, and together you create something even stronger.

“We know Great Britain has one of the best relay squads in the world, and we've consistently won medals on the biggest stages.

“We had relay practice and it was lovely seeing everyone again because we all live in different countries, so we don't get together very often. We caught up, talked about the season.

‌



“It might seem strange to people that we go from being rivals to teammates, but ultimately we all want to win. When we come together, we become even stronger.”

That catch-up with her relay colleagues came just before the Wanda Diamond League event at the London Stadium, where Hunt ran in the 4x100m relay and the 200m.

She was part of a British that won the relay, before having to settle for fifth in a high-class field in the 200m, won by Julien Alfred, the Olympic champion over 100m.

‌



Hunt produced a season’s best of 22.30, a hundredth faster than she had managed at the same event the year before.

She kicked on from that performance to produce the best showing of her career so far when she won World Championship silver in Tokyo last September.

And with her participation in London only confirmed in the days before because of an illness in the build-up that had forced her to cut short a training session, Hunt believes the signs are positive that she could come away with even more individual success this summer.

‌



She added: “It's pretty much the same time I ran here last year, so if anyone's paying attention, they'll know that's a pretty good omen.

“At Christmas I wrote down my goals, and now I'm starting to think, "Wow, maybe we can chase those." I think I'm always a bit of a dark horse going into championships, so no matter what's happened during my season, people should never write me off. I'm excited.”

As a former junior standout – Hunt still holds the world under-18 record for the 200m – this development to the highest level has not come as a complete surprise.

‌



She has achieved it while also studying at the University of Cambridge, from which she graduated in 2023, recovering from a ruptured tendon the previous year, before heading out to Padua, where she now trains.

That has meant putting education on the backburner while she focuses all her attention on athletics, but it remains something she is keen to explore.

She added: “I've always said I'd like to do a master's degree at some point.

‌



“That hasn't happened yet, partly because I now live in a country where I'm still not fluent in the language. But I'd definitely like to return to academia one day because I really enjoy it.

“I'm a human being before I'm an athlete. I want to experience the world, keep learning, grow intellectually, and be inspired by things outside my own little sporting bubble.

I think it's healthy to live as broad a life as possible.

‌



“There was a master's programme at the V&A that I was looking at recently, so perhaps that's something I'll come back to.

“Athletes, particularly women, are increasingly showing that our lives can be much broader than just track. We can study, have careers alongside athletics, and pursue different interests. Life is much bigger than the nine lanes out there.”

Life is bigger than those nine lanes, but when it comes to Birmingham, most of Hunt’s time will be spent racing down them.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Sports.title: Coleman: Ireland's new generation not scarred by past World Cup play-off pain
Sports.content:
Seamus Coleman insists the Republic of Ireland's new generation will not be scarred by the bitter pain of World Cup play-off defeat as they attempt to book a ticket for this summer's finals.

Ireland face the Czech Republic at Prague's Fortuna Arena on Thursday evening attempting to go one better than they did in 2009 against France and in 2017, when Denmark shattered their dreams with a 5-1 demolition job in Dublin.

However, Everton defender Coleman, who was not in the squad on that fateful night in Paris and was injured for the game with the Danes, is confident there will be no hangover, with the Czechs standing between Heimir Hallgrimsson's men and a winner-takes-all match with either Denmark or North Macedonia in Dublin on Tuesday.

Asked if the pain of those near-misses was fuelling the latest bid to make it to the finals for the first time since 2002, the 37-year-old said: "It's difficult to say if it's fuelling the players, they're all so young.
