World.title: Sacked, Scattered, Waiting to Return — Untold story of Plateau’s communities emptied by violence
World.content:
File: Governor Mutfwang in an armoured vehicle during a condolence visit.

By Golok Nanmwa

For decades, Plateau State was celebrated as Nigeria’s “Home of Peace and Tourism,” renowned for its breathtaking hills, fertile farmlands and rich cultural diversity. Communities across the state thrived on agriculture, commerce and peaceful coexistence.

Read Also: 25 children from Kebbi, Kwara, Niger died in terrorists’ captivity — Lawmaker

Today, that identity has been overshadowed by years of recurring violence that have left many rural communities deserted, thousands of residents displaced and vast stretches of farmland abandoned.

Across Bokkos, Barkin Ladi, Riyom, Bassa, Mangu, Jos South, Kanam and Qua’an Pan Local Government Areas, villages that once echoed with children’s laughter, farming activities and bustling markets now bear the scars of repeated attacks.

Homes have been razed, churches and schools destroyed, traditional institutions weakened and thousands of families forced into Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) camps or neighbouring communities.

Governor Caleb Mutfwang recently acknowledged the magnitude of the crisis, disclosing during a television interview that several Plateau communities had been sacked by armed attackers.

According to him, the objective of his administration is not merely to provide temporary humanitarian assistance but to ensure the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced persons to their ancestral homes. That commitment reflects one of the most pressing humanitarian and security challenges confronting Plateau State today.

Communities emptied by violence

Although Plateau has experienced cycles of violence over the years, the attacks recorded in recent times have deepened the humanitarian crisis.

Among the worst-hit local government areas are Bokkos, Barkin Ladi, Riyom, Bassa, Mangu, Jos South, Kanam and Qua’an Pan, where dozens of communities have suffered repeated attacks.

Many displaced residents told Vanguard they have remained away from home for months because they fear fresh attacks and allege that some farmlands and surrounding areas remain occupied by armed groups. For farming families whose livelihoods depended entirely on agriculture, displacement has meant more than losing their homes. It has also meant losing their only source of income.

Mary Pius, a displaced farmer now living in Heipang, Barkin Ladi Local Government Area, said life has become extremely difficult since she fled her community.

“We have lost everything. Our farms are there, but we cannot go back because of fear. We only want peace so we can return home and begin farming again,” she said.

Barkin Ladi: Communities living in fear

Barkin Ladi remains one of Plateau’s major flashpoints. Communities around Ropp, Gashish, Fan, Heipang, Kakuruk, Mazat, Gwol, Fass, Jol, Sabon Layi and surrounding settlements have witnessed repeated attacks over the years.

The July attack on Sabon Layi, where vigilante operatives were reportedly killed, heightened concerns over insecurity despite the deployment of security personnel. It could be recalled that a then serving Senator Gyang Dantong alongside a then member representing Barkin Ladi constituency Hon Gyang Fulani died after attending a mass burial in the local government in July 2012 .Indigenous youth organisations recently commended the Department of State Services (DSS) for establishing an operational base in the area, saying intelligence-driven operations had reduced attacks before fresh violence resurfaced.

The groups alleged that criminal elements had adopted new tactics aimed at frustrating ongoing security operations.

Riyom: “We only want to go home”

Several communities have suffered attacks in Riyom local government. Communities including Kum, Wereng, Rim, Jol, Dyan, Bachi, Nding, Rakok and neighbouring villages have witnessed repeated attacks resulting in deaths, destruction of homes and fresh displacement. Some communities have also been taken over by these bandits. One of the latest attacks reportedly claimed the lives of a three-month-old baby alongside several other residents. Earlier attacks also claimed the lives of women, children and farmers returning from their farms.

Barnabas Mathew, a youth leader in Riyom, said residents remain determined to return to their ancestral communities but insisted that security must first be guaranteed. “We have been sacked from our ancestral communities, but we still want to return home. Government must ensure adequate security. Our appeal is for security operatives to go after those occupying our communities so our people can safely return,” he said.

He commended Governor Caleb Mutfwang for initiating plans to resettle displaced persons, saying the effort had restored hope to many victims. “We appreciate Governor Mutfwang’s commitment to returning displaced people to their ancestral homes. It is encouraging, but lasting peace will only come when those behind these attacks are flushed out completely.”

Another community leader, Danlami Pam, also appealed for sustained military operations across vulnerable communities. “Our people have suffered enough. We are pleading with security agencies to pursue those responsible wherever they are hiding. Once security is guaranteed, our people are ready to return and rebuild their communities.”

Residents insist that while humanitarian support has helped many displaced families survive, nothing compares to returning to their ancestral homes. They described displacement as a painful experience that has separated families, disrupted farming and deprived children of stable education.

Bokkos: A community still mourning

If any local government area symbolises the devastating human cost of Plateau’s insecurity, it is Bokkos. Once known for its thriving farming communities, the area has, over the years, witnessed repeated attacks that have left entire villages deserted, hundreds of families displaced and livelihoods destroyed.

Communities including Hurti, Manguna, Daffo, Ruwi, Mbar, Tangur, Butura Kampani, Sha, Pyakmang, Darwat, Kopmur, Kawel, Mushere and Toff have all experienced varying degrees of violence, forcing thousands of residents to flee. Community leaders estimate that at least nine to 10 villages in Mushere District alone have been largely emptied following repeated attacks, leaving between 15,000 and 19,000 residents displaced.

The humanitarian situation remains dire as many families continue to depend on assistance from government, churches, humanitarian organisations and kind-hearted individuals.

The killing of the Saf Ron-Kulere of Bokkos, Late Lazarus Agaie, about a decade ago further underscored the deteriorating security situation in the area. The first-class traditional ruler was ambushed and killed by gunmen while returning from his farm in Sha District, an incident that shocked the state and renewed calls for stronger protection for traditional institutions.

Several district heads, village heads and community leaders have also lost their lives in separate attacks over the years, leaving many communities without experienced leadership at a time they need it most.

A clergyman, Mr. Henry Godfrey, said the people of Bokkos have endured enormous pain but remain hopeful that peace will return. “We have witnessed communities being completely wiped out. Families have been scattered while thousands now live in makeshift camps. What our people desire is not revenge but peace, justice and the opportunity to return home.”

He lauded Governor Caleb Mutfwang’s determination to facilitate the return of displaced persons to their ancestral communities, describing the initiative as a major step towards restoring hope.

According to him, rebuilding destroyed houses must go hand-in-hand with restoring security if displaced families are to return permanently.

Bassa: Farmers abandon ancestral lands

Bassa Local Government Area has also recorded repeated attacks over the years. Communities around Miango, Zike in Kwall District, Kimakpa, Kpachudu, Hwrra, Ta’agbe, Jebbu Miango, Ancha and Kperie have all suffered varying degrees of violence.

Residents say fear has forced many farmers to abandon thousands of hectares of fertile agricultural land. For many households, farming was the only source of livelihood. Today, many displaced families depend almost entirely on humanitarian assistance and support from relatives.

Community leaders warned that continued displacement could worsen food insecurity across Plateau State because many of the affected communities were major producers of maize, potatoes, vegetables and other food crops.

Mangu and neighbouring communities

Communities in Mangu Local Government Area have also experienced repeated attacks affecting settlements around Mangu Halle, Kombun, Fungzai, Chanso, Tyop, Sabon Gari and communities around the Panyam axis.

Residents say attacks have displaced many families and placed enormous pressure on neighbouring communities receiving displaced persons. Many schools, health centres and places of worship have equally been affected by the insecurity.

The state government has since directed that a comprehensive census be conducted in vulnerable communities as part of efforts to identify legitimate residents, prevent illegal occupation of abandoned settlements and prepare for future resettlement.

Kanam and Qua’an Pan

Communities in Kanam and Qua’an Pan Local Government Areas have also experienced attacks, kidnappings and killings. Residents say they now depend heavily on security patrols, the military and local vigilante groups to protect their communities.

The killing of about 20 security personnel and vigilantes during an ambush in Garga area of Kanam further demonstrated the enormous risks faced by those protecting rural communities. Many residents insist that although security agencies have continued operations, more sustained action is needed to restore confidence among displaced families.

The growing education crisis

Beyond the destruction of homes and farmlands, insecurity is gradually undermining education across many rural communities. In Riyom and Barkin Ladi Local Government Areas particularly, repeated attacks have disrupted academic activities and forced temporary closure of several schools.

Communities such as Shonong, Lwa, Fang, Bangai, Tanjol, Darwat, Daku-Jol and Hei-Gwe Kwi have all experienced disruptions affecting both primary and secondary schools.

Similarly, Government Secondary School, Sho, Government Secondary School, Ropp and Dogo Primary School have all experienced interruptions resulting from insecurity. Parents say attacks or even rumours of attacks are enough to keep children and teachers away from school.

Jennifer Dung, a parent from Riyom, said maintaining a stable academic calendar has become almost impossible. “Lessons are postponed, examinations rescheduled and children are constantly interrupted. Many of them now associate school with fear because they never know when another attack may occur,” she said.

Danlami Pam, another resident, said prolonged school closures have left many children academically behind their counterparts in safer communities. According to him, some pupils now spend weeks out of school whenever attacks occur.

Rwang Tenglong, spokesman of the Berom Youth Moulders, said meaningful educational development cannot take place where insecurity persists. “If our people are not secure, education cannot thrive. Government must first secure lives before children can concentrate on learning,” he said.

Parents who can afford it have relocated to safer communities. Mrs. Kachllom Danlami, who moved from Ropp to Heipang with her family, said the decision was painful but necessary. “Because of the insecurity, I relocated. My child now attends school in Heipang without constant fear. Every parent wants that kind of peace.”

For thousands of other displaced families, however, relocation remains financially impossible. They continue to hope that improved security will enable their children to return to schools within their ancestral communities.

The human cost

Beyond casualty figures lies an even greater tragedy. Thousands of children have had their education disrupted. Farmers have lost access to fertile lands. Women have lost husbands. Children have become orphans. Markets have collapsed. Healthcare facilities have either been destroyed or abandoned.

Traditional rulers have become targets, while vigilante operatives and security personnel continue to pay the ultimate price defending vulnerable communities.

Residents say rebuilding the Plateau will require far more than reconstructing houses. It will require rebuilding confidence, restoring livelihoods and ensuring that communities can once again live without fear.

Government’s response: Returning IDPs to ancestral communities

Recognising that military operations alone cannot solve the crisis, the Plateau State Government says it is pursuing a comprehensive strategy aimed at restoring displaced persons to their ancestral homes.

Governor Caleb Mutfwang has repeatedly stated that the ultimate goal of his administration is not simply to provide temporary relief in Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) camps but to ensure the safe, voluntary and dignified return of victims to their communities.

To actualise that vision, the government established a Resettlement Task Force chaired by retired Air Commodore Christopher Pam to develop a phased roadmap for returning displaced residents.

The administration also received reports from the Land Administration Committee and the Resettlement Task Force to address issues surrounding land ownership, illegal occupation and the rebuilding of affected communities.

As part of the initiative, the governor directed that a comprehensive census be conducted in vulnerable communities, particularly in parts of Mangu Local Government Area, to identify illegal occupants and prevent unauthorised settlements on lands abandoned by displaced residents.

According to the governor, the exercise will assist the government in restoring legitimate owners to their ancestral communities while strengthening security around vulnerable settlements.

The state government is also collaborating with the Federal Government, humanitarian organisations and development partners to mobilise resources for reconstruction and resettlement. Government said the programme includes the rebuilding of residential houses, schools, healthcare facilities and other critical infrastructure destroyed during attacks. The administration has equally strengthened collaboration with the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and other humanitarian agencies to support long-term recovery and community rebuilding.

Governor Mutfwang maintains that rebuilding communities, restoring livelihoods and guaranteeing security remain central to his administration’s peace agenda.

Communities affected

Across Plateau State, many communities have either been attacked, destroyed or largely deserted following years of recurring violence. Among the affected communities are: Bokkos Local Government Area: Hurti, Manguna, Daffo, Ruwi, Maiyanga, Mbar, Tangur, Butura Kampani, Sha, Pyakmang, Darwat, Kopmur, Kawel, Mushere and Toff.

Barkin Ladi Local Government Area: Gashish District communities, Heipang, Ropp, Dorowa Babuje, NTV, Kakuruk, Mazat, Lobiring, Fan, Tahoss, Marit and Dabwak.

Riyom Local Government Area: Jol, Rim, Dyan, Wereng, Bachi, Gako, Sopp, Attakar, Razat and Hoss.

Bassa Local Government Area: Zike in Kwall District, Kimakpa, Kpachudu, Hwrra, Ta’agbe, Miango axis communities, Jebbu Miango, Ancha and Kperie.

Mangu Local Government Area: Mangu Halle, Sabon Gari, Pushit, Kerang, Kombun, Fungzai, Chanso, Tyop and communities around the Panyam axis.

Other affected communities include Gero in Jos South Local Government Area, Rangarasa and Rantya in Jos South, Kwall District communities in Bassa, Nding Sesut community, Ngbra Zongo and Angwan Rukuba in Jos North.

Residents said many of these communities have witnessed mass killings, destruction of homes, churches and food stores, occupation or abandonment of farmlands, displacement of thousands of residents and prolonged humanitarian hardship.

A defining moment for Plateau

For many displaced families, the dream remains simple: to return home.

Across Bokkos, Barkin Ladi, Riyom, Bassa, Mangu, Jos South, Kanam and Qua’an Pan, thousands of families continue to hope that one day they will return to rebuild their homes, cultivate their farms and restore the peaceful lives they once knew.

Mr Habila Rogo, a community leader in Bokkos who spoke to our correspondent said lasting peace will require sustained military operations, improved intelligence gathering, justice for victims, prosecution of perpetrators, reconstruction of destroyed infrastructure and expanded humanitarian support. He called on the federal government to tackle insecurity and ensure lasting peace in the state.

Yet amid the pain, many residents remain hopeful. They say Governor Mutfwang’s commitment to returning displaced persons to their ancestral homes has renewed optimism, but stress that the success of the initiative will ultimately depend on sustained security operations, strong federal support, effective reconstruction and the political will to ensure that every displaced Plateau citizen can once again call home, home.

Vanguard News

World.title: Tinubu’s EFCC directive over Osun govt’s account sparks fresh questions over agency’s independence
World.content:
By Omeiza Ajayi, ABUJA

President Bola Tinubu’s directive to the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission EFCC to vacate the court order freezing the Osun State government’s bank account has raised fresh questions about the anti-graft agency’s independence.

Read Also: ‘I’m embarrassed by timing of EFCC action on Osun govt account – Tinubu

Many Nigerians had taken to the social media to ask whether by fiat, the president can order the EFCC around, wondering whether the anti-graft’s agency inertia in the probes of former Humanitarian affairs Minister, Beta Edu and former Kogi state Governor, Yahaya Bello were due to presidential interference.

Some of those who questioned the president’s action were the African Democratic Congress ADC, its presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar, and a Senior Advocate of Nigeria SAN all weighing in on the implications for the rule of law.

The development followed Tinubu’s directive on Thursday ordering the EFCC to immediately return to court and vacate the order freezing the Osun government’s accounts.

The president said although the commission acted within its statutory powers, the timing of the action — days before the August 15 governorship election — was inappropriate, adding that he felt “deeply embarrassed” by the development because actions of federal agencies are often attributed to the presidency.

Before the president’s intervention, the EFCC had defended the freeze, with Wilson Uwujaren, the commission’s Director of Public Affairs, insisting the action was routine and not politically motivated. He cited a similar restriction placed on Edo State’s accounts before the 2024 governorship election, and said the commission could freeze an account for 72 hours without a court order, arguing it was still within the legal window.

On the constitutional questions raised by the episode, Senior Advocate of Nigeria, Oba Maduabuchi, said the president does not have the power under any law to control the EFCC or the ICPC, but argued that public officers retain discretionary powers to act as they consider necessary in peculiar circumstances.

“It would be wrong for us to hear that the person you are supposed to chase has powers to direct you how to chase him. And to do it publicly,” he said.

He added that the president’s intervention, in his view, was “pardonable” given the risk that the freeze could be perceived as an attempt to influence the Osun election.

Maduabuchi, however, faulted the manner of the president’s intervention, saying it ought to have been handled through the Attorney General rather than a public directive bearing the president’s personal signature.

He also suggested that rather than freezing the entire Osun government account, the EFCC should have pursued the specific funds allegedly diverted to private companies. “Go after the money. Leave Oshun State. The one that is in the account is not missing. Go after the one that has left the account,” he said.

The senior advocate that the episode reflected a broader problem of public trust, noting that unlike in other democracies, statements from Nigerian leaders on political and electoral matters are often met with public disbelief. “Nigerians do not trust their rulers,” he said.

ADC National Publicity Secretary, Bolaji Abdullahi, had welcomed Tinubu’s directive but said the president’s explanation had raised more questions than answers, particularly around his reference to a court order authorising the account freeze.

“What we find most curious about the statement is the President’s repeated reference to an alleged court order authorising the freezing of the Osun State Government’s accounts,” he said.

Abdullahi noted that the EFCC had never publicly claimed to have obtained judicial approval before Tinubu’s intervention, defending its action instead on the basis of its statutory powers and what it described as its “preventive mandate.”

He queried: “The obvious question, therefore, is: where did the President obtain the information that a court order existed? If such an order exists, why was it never mentioned by the EFCC in its statement while defending one of the most controversial actions it has taken in recent times?” He added that either the president was misinformed or had chosen to misrepresent the facts, describing both possibilities as “deeply disturbing.”

In a separate statement issued by his Senior Special Assistant on Public Communication, Phrank Shaibu, Atiku Abubakar described the freezing of the account as a dangerous assault on democracy, insisting there could be no justification for it on the eve of a critical election. “It is impossible to ignore the implications of freezing a state’s principal operational account on the eve of a governorship election. Such an action could disrupt governance, delay salary payments, impede essential public services and create an atmosphere of intimidation that has no place in a democratic society,” he said.

Atiku cautioned anti-corruption agencies against conduct that creates the perception they are being deployed to influence political outcomes, warning that “the selective and politically convenient deployment of state institutions diminishes public trust and weakens the democratic order.”

He linked the development to what he called a pattern of coercive federal actions against opposition-controlled states, citing the earlier withholding of Osun State’s statutory local government allocations, and called on opposition parties and Nigerians committed to constitutional democracy to “close ranks and resist this dangerous drift before it is too late.” In a follow-up statement, Atiku challenged Tinubu to direct the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) to release former Kaduna State Governor Nasir El-Rufai, arguing that the president’s intervention in the Osun matter had demolished the long-held claim that anti-corruption agencies act independently of the presidency.

“Having now demonstrated that he can issue direct operational directives to anti-corruption agencies whenever he considers it expedient, President Tinubu owes Nigerians an explanation as to why he cannot exercise the same authority in the case of Mallam Nasir El-Rufai,” he said.

Atiku argued that the president could not simultaneously deny interference in EFCC operations while directing the commission’s next move, describing the arrangement as “executive control disguised as independence” rather than institutional autonomy.

World.title: Why Atiku is worried over strange payment into his bank account
World.content:
Alhaji Atiku Abubakar

By Emmanuel Aziken

Fresh details have emerged on why former Vice President Atiku Abubakar is deeply concerned over a strange payment made into his personal bank account, with fears that the transaction could be part of an attempt to associate him with individuals or activities unknown to him.

Read Also: Atiku raises alarm over mysterious credit alert, suspected data breach

Saturday Vanguard gathered that beyond the unsolicited payment itself, concerns have arisen over the identity and possible motives of the sender, particularly against the backdrop of the description attached to the transaction: “Contribution Electioneering Campaign.”

Atiku, through his spokesman, Phrank Shaibu, had raised the alarm after discovering the payment, insisting that neither the former Vice President nor his political organisation solicited or authorised it.

“Neither His Excellency nor his campaign solicited, authorised or has any knowledge of the individual or entity behind the unauthorised payment,” Shaibu said in a statement.

However, Saturday Vanguard gathered that one of the major concerns surrounding the transaction is the possibility that unsolicited funds could be used to create a financial trail linking the former Vice President to persons or activities with which he has no connection.

There are fears within Atiku’s camp that unexplained payments could potentially expose the recipient to questions over links to terrorism financing, drug trafficking, fraud or other criminal activities, particularly where the true source and purpose of the funds remain unknown.

There is, however, no evidence presently available to Saturday Vanguard that the money originated from any terrorist, drug trafficking or other criminal organisation. The concern is over the potential implications of receiving unexplained funds and the possibility that such transactions could subsequently be used to create damaging associations.

How Did Sender Get Atiku’s Account Details?

Another source of worry is how the sender obtained Atiku’s personal banking details in the first place.

According to the earlier statement by Shaibu, the account into which the money was paid is strictly personal and its details are not publicly available.

“The account is a strictly private one whose details are not in the public domain. This raises a fundamental question: How did unknown persons obtain the confidential banking details of a private citizen?” the statement said.

Saturday Vanguard gathered that there are concerns that the account information, which may ordinarily be accessible to the bank and relevant financial regulatory institutions in the course of their statutory responsibilities, could have been improperly disclosed.

Atiku’s camp has consequently raised questions over whether somebody with privileged access to sensitive financial information may have been responsible for exposing the details.

“Even more disturbing is the suspicion that such confidential information may have been obtained through persons with privileged access,” the statement said.

Bank Launches Investigation

Saturday Vanguard gathered that the bank involved, one of Nigeria’s top five banks, has launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the transaction.

The bank was expected to revert to Atiku with its findings at the weekend as efforts continued to establish how the transaction occurred and, crucially, whether it could help identify its origin.

Further checks by Saturday Vanguard indicated that the money was transferred from an OPay account, potentially adding another layer to efforts to establish the identity behind the payment.

While transactions conducted through regulated financial platforms ordinarily leave records that may assist investigations, Atiku’s concern remains that the person immediately associated with the transfer may not necessarily reveal who ultimately initiated or motivated it.

Wider Security Concerns

The former Vice President believes the implications extend beyond his personal circumstances.

“If the private banking information of a former Vice President and a leading presidential candidate can be accessed and deployed for reasons yet unknown then no Nigerian’s financial privacy is safe,” the statement quoted him as saying.

Atiku also warned that unauthorised access to confidential financial information could create potentially serious security vulnerabilities for ordinary Nigerians.

“If established, this would amount to a grave abuse of power capable of exposing the account holder to kidnappers, terrorists, bandits, fraudsters and other criminal elements,” the statement added.

For Atiku, therefore, the mystery is not simply about money unexpectedly appearing in his account.

The questions are who sent it, why it was labelled an electioneering campaign contribution, how the sender obtained details of a private account and what purpose the transaction was intended to serve. Those questions have assumed greater significance given Atiku’s status as a former Vice President and prominent opposition politician ahead of the 2027 general elections.

According to his spokesman, the matter has already been brought to the attention of security agencies and the Nigerian public.

His camp views the development as one of a number of suspicious incidents in the political environment ahead of 2027 and wants the source of the payment, as well as how the sender obtained the account details, conclusively established.

Until those questions are answered, the strange deposit is being treated not as a windfall but as a potential security and political red flag.

World.title: 25 children from Kebbi, Kwara, Niger died in terrorists’ captivity — Lawmaker
World.content:
Woro victims receiving medical attention at Kwara State University Teaching Hospital, Ilorin, Friday. Photo: Demola Akinyemi.

••• 12 youths joined terrorists’ army; two pregnant women returned with babies; Woro attack sad, regrettable — Gov AbdulRazaq

By Demola Akinyemi, Ilorin

Twenty five children who were among the 336 persons kidnapped by the terrorists in Kebbi, Kwara and Niger states died in captivity and they were buried in the forest.

Read Also: Tinubu, Wike, Akume listed as PFIPC board members, Reps raise questions

Lawmaker representing Gwanabe/Gweria/Bani/Adena state constituency of Kaiama local government in the Kwara State House of Assembly, Hon. Saidu Baba-Ahmed disclosed this yesterday while speaking on the conditions of the 315 kidnap victims who regained their freedom on Thursday night after spending six months in captivity.

The figure comprises 308 victims rescued from terrorist captivity in the forests of Kwara and Niger states and seven students of Gateway ICT Polytechnic, Saapade in Ogun state who were abducted last week.

The lawmaker, in an interview told Saturday Vanguard that 12 of the youths joined the terrorists’ army and were not among those released by the terrorists. According to him, “The terrorists asked the youths who among them would like to join their army and 12 of them volunteered to join them. So, those youths are not among those who were released.

“25 children from Kebbi, Niger and Kwara states also died in captivity and some died in transit and they were buried there. A total of 176 victims were kidnapped from Kwara state and 163 regained their freedom. 15 of the victims are still missing now.

“Also, none of the women came with pregnancy but two women who were kidnapped with pregnancy came back with two babies. We checked them properly and discovered that none of them is pregnant, because they told us that their abductors didn’t touch them. But two women who were abducted with pregnancy came back with two babies“.

Hon. Saidu Baba-Ahmed said that those who were set free arrived in Ilorin, the Kwara state capital and 46 of them were receiving medical attention at the hospital. He also said that the state government was taking care of them to ascertain their state of health before reuniting them with their families.

The lawmaker then commended the state and the federal governments for their efforts in ensuring that the abductees returned home safely.

The victims who were abducted during the deadly attack on Woro community in Kaiama Local Government Area of Kwara State were received at the Nigerian Army’s 2 Division, Sobi Barracks, Ilorin before being moved to an undisclosed location where they spent the night.

The victims were kidnapped when armed terrorists invaded the community on February 3 this year, killing scores of residents and whisking away the victims into the forest, triggering widespread outrage and intensified security operations. Following sustained military operations and coordinated efforts by security agencies, the victims regained their freedom and were transported from Niger State to Ilorin late Thursday night.

The rescued victims were expected to be officially handed over to Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, who has consistently engaged security authorities to ensure their safe return.

Their arrival marks a major breakthrough in the months-long efforts to secure the release of the abductees, while authorities continue to verify the number of those rescued and provide necessary care and support.

Meanwhile, Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq of Kwara state while receiving the victims of Woro attack in Ilorin yesterday described the February bloody event as not only sad, but regrettable. The governor received the victims who are mostly kids and women, from the 22 Armoured Brigade Commander Brigadier General Nicholas Rume.

Mallam AbdulRazaq also hailed President Bola Tinubu for his swift response and assistance to the state. He added that the president had approved the establishment of five Army Battalions in Omu-Aran, Patigi, Ilemona, Kosubosu and Kaiama.
