World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.

World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: Venezuelan government and opposition open US-backed talks
World.content:
Venezuelan government and opposition open US-backed talks

7th Friday, August 2026 - 21:17 UTC Full article

The government and opposition delegations during the first meeting at the La Carlota Convention Center in Caracas

Delegations from the Venezuelan government and one sector of the opposition met on Thursday in Caracas to open negotiations backed by the United States, in the first face-to-face encounter since Nicolás Maduro's detention by US forces on January 3.

The meeting was held behind closed doors at the La Carlota Convention Center, in the Sucre municipality, with no press access. In an identical statement issued by both sides, the teams announced they would remain in permanent session until Wednesday, August 12, when they will decide whether the plenary continues.

The text sets out the agreed principles: respect for national sovereignty, good-faith negotiation, a political, peaceful, democratic and constitutional solution, mutual recognition, equality and parity at the table, verifiable compliance with commitments, and protection of the human and political rights of all forces.

The government delegation is led by Jorge Rodríguez, president of the National Assembly and brother of acting President Delcy Rodríguez. He is accompanied by lawmakers Pedro Infante, América Pérez, Génesis Garvett and Jorge Arreaza, along with Higher Education Minister Ana María San Juan.

The opposition delegation is headed by Dinorah Figuera, president of the National Assembly elected in 2015, which the United States regards as the last democratically elected institution in the country. Figuera, a 65-year-old physician and member of Primero Justicia, had led that chamber from exile in Spain and returned to Venezuela on Wednesday; the Venezuelan government had issued an arrest warrant against her after her election in 2023. Her delegation includes Marco Aurelio Quiñones, Desiree Barboza, Ramón López, Jorge Millán and Juan Miguel Matheus.

The agenda covers three areas: assistance for those affected by June's earthquakes, strengthening democracy, and guarantees for political and civil rights. The opposition is seeking a restructuring of the National Electoral Council and the Supreme Court, the lifting of bans on political parties, a timetable for presidential, regional and parliamentary elections, and the release of political prisoners. None of those points has been agreed.

The State Department issued a statement while the meeting was under way describing the direct talks as a unique opportunity and reiterating its commitment to supporting a Venezuelan-led process, as part of a three-phase plan aimed at stabilization, economic recovery, political reconciliation and a peaceful transition.

The process faces resistance. Opposition leader María Corina Machado has been left out and has said she was not consulted, while stating she will not obstruct it. On the government side, Diosdado Cabello played down the initiative, saying there are talks in the country every day.

World.title: Why the Falkland Islands are British
World.content:
Why the Falkland Islands are British

7th Friday, August 2026 - 20:58 UTC Full article

The islands are not an “imperial possession” of Britain – that’s 19th-century language. Photo: Getty Images

By Graham Pascoe (*)



On 11 July 2026 the Argentine foreign minister, Pablo Quirno, wrote a long article on the Falkland Islands (or the Malvinas, as they are called in Spanish) in the Buenos Aires newspaper La Nación, as Iona Cleave reported in the London Telegraph the next day. On 23 July he published an almost identical article in the Israeli English-language daily Jerusalem Post. In both his articles the foreign minister repeated several arguments which (he said) showed the strength of Argentina's claim to the Falklands. Unfortunately for him, everything he said is historically and legally untrue, as will be pointed out below.

Mr Quirno chose to write at this particular juncture because of the clash between Argentina and England in the football World Cup, and also because in April President Trump asked the Pentagon to “review Britain’s claim to the Falkland Islands”, as a possible “punishment” for Britain’s unwillingness to support his war on Iran (as the Telegraph reported on 24 April). The Pentagon was apparently considering various options, including reassessing “diplomatic support for long-standing European ‘imperial possessions’ such as the Falkland Islands”. The story appeared in all major Argentine newspapers, and follow-up articles have appeared in various media since then.

I feel it’s important to get things straight before taking this too seriously, so here are some basic facts about Britain’s claim to the Falklands, which will demonstrate the untruth of Mr Quirno’s assertions.

To begin with, the islands are not an “imperial possession” of Britain – that’s 19th-century language. In the 19th century Britain simply possessed the Falklands, just as other colonial powers possessed their imperial possessions. But since the Second World War the steady development of the international law of decolonisation has decisively changed the position. International decolonisation law is contained in the United Nations Charter, UN Resolutions, and rulings by the International Court of Justice. Under all of those things, Britain is no longer the possessor of the Falklands, but only the “administering power”; the islands’ inhabitants, the Falkland Islanders, hold the full right of self-determination and are the ultimate arbiters of their country’s destiny.

United Nations General Assembly Resolution 1541 of 1960 lays down three ways in which decolonisation may take place. It may lead to:

(1) Independence;

(2) Free association with an independent state; or

(3) Integration with an independent state.

Resolution 2625 of 1970 repeats those three options and adds the so-called “fourth option”:

(4) The emergence into any other political status freely determined by a people.

To add a word of explanation: (1) “independence” would mean that the Falklands would become a sovereign country, eligible for membership of the United Nations, with embassies abroad and with foreign embassies in Stanley; (2) “free association” would mean that the Falklands would become an independent country with full control over all domestic policy but with its defence and some aspects of its foreign policy delegated to Britain. An example of free association is the Republic of Palau, a small island country in the Pacific with some 350 islands and around 18,000 people; it has been a UN member state since 1994, but it is in “free association” with the United States, which provides its defence since it has no armed forces of its own; (3) “integration” would mean the Falklands would become part of Britain, i.e. part of some British constituency (say in Cornwall), and would vote for an MP in British elections. Both (2) and (3) would naturally require Britain’s approval too. And (4) “any other status” is what the Falklands now have in international law, under UN Resolution 2625.

The constitutional progress of the Falklands since 1945, with new constitutions in 1949, 1985 and 2009, has brought a steady increase in the participation of the Falkland Islanders in the governance of their country, and the referendum of 2013 showed that they have “freely determined” the political status they wish to have under UN Resolution 2625, i.e. partnership with Britain. The referendum was organised entirely by the Falkland Islands Government, not by Britain – in fact Britain took no part in it whatever, and the British government was happy to allow the Falkland Islanders to use it to exercise their right to self-determination. The islands’ status could of course change at any time, but only in accordance with the wishes of the Falkland Islanders. So in any discussion of the Falklands, it should be stressed that under international law their status conforms to United Nations Resolutions 1541 and 2625.

The International Court of Justice has stated in several of its rulings, for example its Advisory Opinions in the Namibia case in 1971 and the Chagos Islands case in 2019, that “the subsequent development of international law in regard to non-self-governing territories, as enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations, made the principle of self-determination applicable to all of them”. That naturally includes the Falklands; any assertion that they are not covered by decolonisation law (for example because they are the subject of a territorial dispute) is untrue.

The history of the islands’ relations with the outside world reveals that Argentina gave up its partial claim to the islands in the 19th century, and confirmed its renunciation on several occasions.

In the pivotal year 1833, when Britain expelled the Argentine garrison, which had murdered its commanding officer in cold blood and had terrified and traumatised the civilian inhabitants, there was no international consensus on who the islands belonged to. The islands were a disputed territory: Argentina regarded the Falklands as 100% Argentinian; Britain regarded them as 100% British; Spain still regarded them as 100% Spanish (but accepted significant British rights under the 1771 Anglo-Spanish treaty and the 1790 Nootka Sound Convention) – and the United States denied all those claims and held that the islands were terra nullius (“no man’s land”). To the United States they were part of the high seas, belonging to no country, and were open to all. So in 1833 it was unclear who owned the Falklands – or indeed whether anyone owned them at all.

The view of the United States changed during the 19th century, and in 1875, when the US appointed George Gerard as US Consul in Stanley, the US ceased to regard the islands as part of the high seas and recognised that they were under British sovereignty. Consular recognition was the highest level of international recognition the islands could be accorded, since they were not a sovereign country. From the 1850s to the 1970s there were ten countries that at various times accorded the Falklands consular recognition: Belgium, Chile, Denmark, France, Italy, Germany, Norway, Sweden, the United States and Uruguay. Each of those countries had a consulate in Stanley for many years. Norway holds the record for length of consular representation with almost 100 years, from 1877 to 1974; the United States was represented for 33 years from 1875 to 1908, while the other countries were represented for several decades – Uruguay, for example, had a consulate in Stanley for over 50 years from 1924 to 1975.

For 17 years, from 1833 to 1849 inclusive, Argentina protested annually against Britain’s possession of the islands, thus keeping the Falklands dispute alive and maintaining the Argentine claim (which was always only partial, of course, since it was limited by the equally valid, but likewise partial, claims of other countries).

But in 1850 there was a radical change. In that year Britain and Argentina ratified the Convention of Peace, an all-embracing peace treaty between the two countries, signed on 24 November 1849 and brought into effect by its ratification by both sides on 15 May 1850. That treaty ended a British military intervention around the River Plate and established “perfect friendship” between Britain and Argentina. That ended the Falklands dispute. “Perfect friendship” naturally ruled out the existence of any dispute between the two countries.

It is impossible to reconcile the 1850 Convention of Peace with any idea of a continuing Argentine claim to the Falkland Islands. That was clearly accepted by Argentina. For example, Argentine President Bartolomeo Mitre, in his speech opening the Argentine Congress on 1 May 1865, said that some outstanding claims by Britain and France had been settled, so that now “there was nothing to prevent the consolidation of friendly relations between this country and those Governments”. So there was no dispute with Britain, such as that over the Falkland Islands.

A year later the Vice-President of Argentina, Marcos Paz, in opening the Argentine Congress on 1 May 1866, was even more specific: he mentioned some outstanding compensation claims by British citizens, and said: “This question, which is the only one between us and the British nation, has not yet been settled.” So apart from those private claims, there were no issues between Britain and Argentina – there was no dispute over the Falkland Islands. And four years later on 1 May 1869, in his speech opening the Argentine Congress, President Domingo Sarmiento said “Nothing is claimed from us by other nations; we have nothing to ask of them”. So Argentina had nothing to claim from Britain, and thus had no claim to the Falkland Islands.

Accordingly, Argentina ceased to protest against Britain’s possession of the Falklands for 38 years, from 1849 to 1888, and after a brief revival of a claim in 1888 dropped it again and has never delivered a formal protest since then. Some apologists for Argentina have pointed out that Argentina made one last protest on 29 December 1849, after the Convention of Peace was signed, but that was of course in the “limbo” period between the signing and the ratification of the treaty. During that time the treaty was not yet in force (in the 19th century treaties only came into force upon ratification), so Argentina could protest without invalidating the peace treaty. Once it had been ratified in 1850 Argentina’s protests ceased.

So the Falklands dispute ended on 15 May 1850. That is well known in Argentina, and it has been accepted many times by Spanish-speaking authors, for example by the Mexican historian Carlos Pereyra in a book published in Spain in 1919 and reprinted in Argentina in 1944, by the Argentine historian Ernesto Fitte in two books published in Argentina in 1974 and 1975, by the Argentine historian Alfredo Burnet-Merlín in a book published in Argentina in 1974, and most recently by the Argentine historian Juan José Cresto in a two-volume work published in Argentina in 2011, when he was President of the Argentine Academy of History – he complains bitterly that the Convention of Peace established “perfect friendship” between Britain and Argentina but did not do anything to hand the Falklands to Argentina.

There are many other significant facts that demonstrate that Argentina has no claim whatsoever to the Falklands – to take only two examples, Argentina issued maps in the 1880s that showed the Falkland Islands as being outside Argentina, and in 1899-1902 and again in 1964-66 twice accepted arbitration by Britain over the line of the border between Argentina and Chile, thus accepting Britain as being qualified to rule on what was Argentine territory and what was not.

All those acts by Argentina over more than 150 years, plus United Nations Resolutions 1541 and 2625, demonstrate that the Falkland Islands are British territory in international law and the Falkland Islanders possess the full right of internal and external self-determination, so they are the ultimate decision-makers on the future of their country. Those are the legal and historical facts of the case.

In contrast to those, Mr Quirno repeated untrue statements in both his recent articles, which have constituted the Argentine case for several decades. He said in his article in La Nación:

“In 1833 the United Kingdom occupied the islands by means of an act of force never accepted by our country, disrupted Argentina’s territorial integrity, expelled our national authorities and the legitimately established population, proceeded to populate the territory with its own citizens and prevented the settlement of Argentine citizens.” (Quote from Pablo Quirno in La Nación, Buenos Aires, 11 July 2026; almost identical text in article by Pablo Quirno in Jerusalem Post, 23 July 2026)

Every word of that is untrue. Here are the facts:

- In 1833 a single British ship, HMS Clio, ordered the lowering of the Argentine flag and the raising of the Union Jack at Port Louis, the then capital of the islands. There was no force, no one was injured, and the Clio simply sailed away without leaving any British forces. There was no official British presence for a whole year after that.

- Britain did not expel the Argentine “national authorities”, nor the population. Britain expelled only the Argentine garrison of 26 soldiers, with their 11 female camp-followers and eight children. The soldiers had mutinied, murdered their commanding officer in cold blood, and robbed and terrorised the civilian inhabitants, of whom there were exactly 37. Eight civilians had fled from the violence of the Argentine soldiers and taken refuge aboard a British seal-hunting ship that was there at the time. Britain did not expel the civilians but encouraged them to stay, and 22 of them did so.

- Britain’s action in 1833 was in fact accepted by Argentina. Argentina confirmed this by ratifying the Convention of Peace in 1850 and by many subsequent acts, including top-level statements by Argentine leaders, the publication of maps showing the Falklands as outside Argentina and the acceptance of Britain as qualified to rule on the extent of Argentina’s territory.

- Britain did not disrupt Argentina’s territorial integrity. As explained above, there was no consensus as to whose territory the islands were. Only Argentina saw them as Argentine territory; Britain saw them as British territory (in Britain’s view, Britain had simply expelled an illegal garrison); Spain saw them as Spanish territory, and the United States saw them as part of the high seas and therefore no one’s territory.

- Britain did not populate the islands with its own citizens. Today’s Falkland Islanders are from many countries; several families who have been in the islands for 7, 8, or even 9 generations are descended originally from Norwegian, Swedish, Danish, German, French or Finnish immigrants in the 19th century. And several ancestors of modern Falkland Islanders arrived by being shipwrecked in the islands – some of them literally swam ashore. Britain did not “introduce” them.

- Britain has never prevented Argentine citizens from settling in the Falklands. There have almost always been Argentine citizens in the islands (there are some now), and the largest group of people who arrived in the whole of the 19th century were 117 people who arrived aboard the Norwegian ship Napoleon from Montevideo on 10 May 1847, including 17 Argentinians and 15 Uruguayans, who were permitted to settle and work in the Falklands. There have been many others since.

Those, then, are the facts of the Falklands case. Mr Quirno’s contentions are without foundation, and the Falkland Islands are British territory in international law.

Graham Pascoe, August 2026

* Graham Pascoe is the author of “The Falklands Saga” (5 vols.; vols. 4 and 5 forthcoming) and “Falklands Facts and Fallacies”.

World.title: Argentine Senate passes property bill after dropping two key chapters
World.content:
Argentine Senate passes property bill after dropping two key chapters

7th Friday, August 2026 - 10:58 UTC Full article

La Libertad Avanza had removed on Wednesday the chapter easing rural land purchases by foreigners, following opposition from several allied governors

Argentina's Senate approved in the early hours of Friday, by 37 votes to 33, the Inviolability of Private Property bill promoted by Deregulation Minister Federico Sturzenegger, after the governing bloc withdrew the two chapters that drew the most resistance. The text now goes to the Chamber of Deputies.

The session ran more than eleven hours and there were no abstentions. La Libertad Avanza had removed on Wednesday the chapter easing rural land purchases by foreigners, following opposition from several allied governors. Minutes before the vote it also gave way on the reform of the Fire Management Law, having found it lacked the votes.

That law bars any change of use for 60 years on native or planted forests, wetlands and protected areas affected by fires, whether accidental or deliberate, and for 30 years on farmland, prairies, grasslands and scrub. The reform would have removed those bans and kept the restriction only for native forests. Senator Edith Terenzi, who chairs the Environment Committee, said the chapter was regressive and contravened the Escazú Agreement.

The approved text retains the reforms on evictions, expropriations and the Real Estate Property Registry. On evictions it introduces an expedited procedure, early restitution of a property where the claimed right appears plausible, and electronic service of notifications. On expropriations it establishes that public utility must be interpreted restrictively and meet criteria of suitability, necessity and proportionality, and sets as the reference for valuing an asset the moment immediately before any state action that might alter its price.

The governing bloc's leader, Patricia Bullrich, defended the bill as a guarantee for those who own a home, a business or a farm. Peronist senators sought to return the bill to committee, a motion rejected by 38 votes to 31. Senator Marcelo Lewandowski counted 17 modifications to the committee report since it was signed and criticized the handling of the process; Martín Soria argued the expropriations chapter aims to make any future attempt to recover privatized companies more costly.

At the start of the session, Senator Juliana Di Tullio asked that governing-party legislator Joaquín Benegas Lynch recuse himself, on the grounds that he owns Glocal Terra, a firm engaged in farm management and advising buyers. The senator rejected the request, arguing that the Public Ethics Law requires a direct and singular interest rather than a benefit shared across an entire sector. Bullrich backed that position.

The chamber also denied remote participation requested by Senator Anabel Fernández Sagasti, who is in advanced pregnancy, and by Radical senator Flavio Fama, recovering from surgery. Both requests were referred to the Constitutional Affairs Committee on a motion by Bullrich, approved by a show of hands.

Bartolomé Abdala presided over the session because Vice President Victoria Villarruel was acting head of the executive during Javier Milei's trip to Ecuador. There were incidents outside Congress during the demonstration called against the bill.

World.title: Milei promotes a summit of right-wing presidents outside existing regional bodies
World.content:
Milei promotes a summit of right-wing presidents outside existing regional bodies

7th Friday, August 2026 - 10:43 UTC Full article

Milei held a bilateral meeting with his Ecuadorian counterpart, Daniel Noboa, at the Carondelet Palace, in the first official visit by an Argentine president to Quito in nearly two decades

Argentine President Javier Milei is working to convene a summit of right-wing leaders from across the Americas outside existing multilateral organizations, though no date has been set. The initiative comes amid a series of trips that took him this week to Ecuador and Colombia.

Milei held a bilateral meeting on Thursday with his Ecuadorian counterpart, Daniel Noboa, at the Carondelet Palace, in the first official visit by an Argentine president to Quito in nearly two decades. The two signed six cooperation instruments: an automotive trade protocol, agreements on air connectivity and tourism, an extradition treaty, cooperation on peaceful uses of nuclear energy, cyberdefense, and a joint declaration against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, providing for information sharing and technical coordination.

The extradition treaty replaces the 1933 Montevideo Convention in the bilateral relationship and must complete domestic approval procedures before taking effect. It will not apply to cases already under way. The governments also agreed to prepare a bilateral cooperation program for 2027-2029.

On the diplomatic front, Noboa reiterated Ecuador's support for Argentina's sovereignty claim over the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, and called for the dispute to be settled through peaceful negotiations. Milei thanked him for that position. The archipelago is a British Overseas Territory; in a 2013 referendum its residents voted overwhelmingly to retain that status.

Trade runs at a deficit for Ecuador. Between January and May 2026 it exported 129.7 million dollars' worth of goods to Argentina and imported 374.5 million, leaving a negative balance of 244.8 million, 11.6% lower than a year earlier, according to Ecuador's central bank. The narrowing reflects a sharper drop in imports than in Ecuadorian sales.

The Quito agenda included a wreath-laying at Independence Square and a meeting between Milei and representatives of Argentine automotive chambers, while Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno took part in the opening of an economic forum. Noboa and Milei then traveled together to Cali for the inauguration of Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, with whom the Argentine leader was scheduled to hold a private meeting. He was also due to meet there with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar.

The trips follow his appearance at the Liberal Party convention in São Paulo, where he backed Flávio Bolsonaro's candidacy, and at Keiko Fujimori's inauguration in Peru. Quirno confirmed this week that the Argentine government is organizing a summit of right-wing presidents in Buenos Aires this year.

Relations between Milei and Noboa have had their ups and downs. In 2024, in an interview published by The New Yorker, the Ecuadorian president sharply criticized his Argentine counterpart, remarks he later softened.

For Argentine sociologist Juan Gabriel Tokatlian, the region's new right-wing governments share affinities with Milei but also have their own ambitions for influence. Whatever Milei's personal ambition, he said, he will find that no one is waiting to be led by him, adding that Latin America is marked by a leadership vacuum because the decisive interlocutor for every country remains the United States.

World.title: Colombia: De la Espriella takes office in Cali without Petro present
World.content:
Colombia: De la Espriella takes office in Cali without Petro present

7th Friday, August 2026 - 10:40 UTC Full article

The 47-year-old criminal defense lawyer won the June 21 runoff against left-wing candidate Iván Cepeda, having never held public office or stood for election before

Abelardo de la Espriella takes office as president of Colombia on Friday at a ceremony held at the Santiago de Cali University, outside Bogotá and without the attendance of his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, in a handover marked by confrontation between the two men.

The 47-year-old criminal defense lawyer won the June 21 runoff against left-wing candidate Iván Cepeda, having never held public office or stood for election before. He will govern until 2030 alongside Vice President José Manuel Restrepo, an economist and former trade and finance minister under Iván Duque.

Petro announced in July that he would neither attend nor shake his successor's hand, accusing him of reaching power through electoral fraud. He has presented no evidence to judicial authorities. National registrar Hernán Penagos Giraldo said on August 5 that there are no doubts about the results; the National Electoral Council upheld the count and the Council of State confirmed both the election and the inauguration venue. The outgoing president's absence does not affect the act's validity: the constitution requires the presence of Congress, not of the departing president.

The venue was disputed. De la Espriella had sought to be sworn in at a military garrison in the south of the country; Petro, as commander of the armed forces until the handover, barred the use of military facilities. Congress ultimately approved the university venue in Cali. The president-elect defended the choice as a sign of decentralization.

Cepeda said he would not attend either and announced peaceful civil disobedience actions, with demonstrations called for the same day. Security operations were deployed at Cali's airport and at key points in the city. Foreign delegations include the vice president of El Salvador.

The incoming government inherits deteriorating security across large areas, with armed groups financed by drug trafficking, illegal mining and extortion, a substantial fiscal deficit and a crisis in the health system. De la Espriella has pledged to build large prisons, refuse negotiations with any armed group and secure the capture or death of five significant leaders within three months, as well as to cut the size of the state by 40% and lower taxes. He has said he will make Barranquilla an alternate capital and that Medellín and Cali will also serve as seats of government.

The designated cabinet combines technical profiles from the established right with figures close to Christian movements. The incoming president has spoken of prosecuting Petro and called the outgoing government coup-minded, accusing it without evidence of corruption. Before entering politics, De la Espriella was known for high-profile litigation and, according to El País, for having advised paramilitary groups in their negotiations with Álvaro Uribe's government more than twenty years ago.

The date coincides with the anniversary of the Battle of Boyacá, on which Colombian presidents traditionally take office.

World.title: Police disperse march against property bill with tear gas, rubber bullets and water cannon
World.content:
Police disperse march against property bill with tear gas, rubber bullets and water cannon

7th Friday, August 2026 - 10:06 UTC Full article

According to police sources, the Federal Police arrested three people and the Buenos Aires City Police another nine, all charged with assault and resisting authority

Twelve people were detained on Thursday during clashes outside Argentina's Congress, at a demonstration called against the Inviolability of Private Property bill being debated in the Senate.

According to police sources, the Federal Police arrested three people and the Buenos Aires City Police another nine, all charged with assault and resisting authority. The Security Ministry deployed some 820 officers from federal forces and the city police under its anti-picket protocol.

Casualty figures remain provisional. Four officers were reported injured, among them a gendarme struck in the head by a stone and taken to the Churruca hospital. Among demonstrators, at least two were hit by rubber bullets, several were affected by tear gas and one man sustained a serious eye injury. The Buenos Aires Press Union and the Association of Press Photographers also reported that a photojournalist suffered a head wound with heavy bleeding and was treated at the Argerich hospital; the cause of the blow has not been established.

Accounts of how the clashes began diverge. According to EFE, the demonstration proceeded without incident until security forces, positioned behind the barriers, began firing tear gas, rubber bullets and water from cannon trucks. Other outlets say confrontations started after a group brought down one of the barriers. La Nación placed the turning point at around 5 p.m., after nearly six hours of peaceful protest, when Federal Police used gas against those pressing on the fencing. A patrol car's windows were smashed, waste containers were set alight and pavements were damaged at several intersections in central Buenos Aires.

The rally began at midday despite rain and brought together the CGT labor federation, both CTA union groupings, the UTEP grassroots workers' union, teachers' unions, Peronist and left-wing organizations, students and unaffiliated citizens, under the slogans “The homeland is not for sale” and “The land is not for sale, not to be burned, not to be evicted from.” Simultaneous demonstrations took place in La Plata, Rosario, Córdoba, Mendoza, Tucumán, Bariloche and Ushuaia.

The protest went ahead even though the governing bloc had withdrawn the previous day the chapter easing rural land purchases by foreigners. “We want this law not to prosper, not only the part about land but also the burning of forests and rents,” Sergio Alarcón, a member of a Peronist organization, told EFE. Deregulation Minister Federico Sturzenegger defended the withdrawn chapter and said he regretted its exclusion.

The Senate approved the bill in the early hours of Friday by 37 votes to 33, after also dropping the chapter amending the Fire Management Law. The text retains the reforms on evictions, expropriations and the Real Estate Property Registry, and now goes to the Chamber of Deputies.

World.title: Two months from the vote, Lula turns diplomatic crises into a sovereignty message
World.content:
Two months from the vote, Lula turns diplomatic crises into a sovereignty message

6th Thursday, August 2026 - 22:08 UTC Full article

Lula links that pressure to the former president's family

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva enters the final stretch toward the October 4 elections with three open diplomatic fronts and a message centered on defending national sovereignty.

The most serious comes from Washington. This week, Donald Trump's administration revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa, citing Brasília's delay in granting approval to its own ambassadorial nominee. Lula called the measure irresponsible and unthinkable between two countries with more than two centuries of diplomatic relations, and said Brazil wants to be treated with respect. Itamaraty described it as part of a deliberate escalation and attributed to Washington an interest in interfering in the election.

Days earlier, Brazil had denied visas to two State Department envoys. The Brazilian government says they intended to join a disinformation strategy aimed at questioning the reliability of the electoral system; Washington says they sought to visit the country ahead of the vote. Neither account has been substantiated. Brasília also fears a large-scale false news campaign on social media, compounded by the use of artificial intelligence.

The episode adds to the trade dispute. The United States imposed 25% tariffs on Brazilian goods citing unfair competition, among other grounds the development of the Pix payment system, which is cutting into US companies' earnings, and Brazilian efforts to regulate large technology firms. A further 12.5% duty over alleged forced labor followed, which the Brazilian government also rejected. A year ago, Washington imposed 50% tariffs during the trial of Jair Bolsonaro, later sentenced to 27 years for attempting a coup, along with sanctions on the judge who led the proceedings.

Lula links that pressure to the former president's family. He refers to its members as traitors to the homeland for putting personal interests, in his view, ahead of the country's economy. Former lawmaker Eduardo Bolsonaro lives in the United States and has spent more than a year pressing for sanctions against Brazil.

“US interference ends up benefiting Lula, especially if the government manages to pin on Flávio Bolsonaro the responsibility he bore in that process,” said Leonardo Paz Neves, a researcher at the Getúlio Vargas Foundation. That is the analyst's reading; the most recent Datafolha poll gave Lula a five-point lead over the senator in a potential runoff.

The second front is Argentina. After Javier Milei's insults in São Paulo, Brazil downgraded relations to chargé d'affaires level and postponed its ambassador's return.

The third, less visible, is Paraguay. Asunción summoned Brazilian Ambassador José Antonio Marcondes de Carvalho and handed him a protest note over Lula's remarks on the War of the Triple Alliance. Paraguay's foreign minister said the two presidents spoke by phone; CNN Brasil reported that Brazilian government figures deny any such conversation. The 1864-1870 conflict had devastating demographic and economic consequences for Paraguay, though estimates of its scale vary widely.

Lula has increased his references to defense in recent days, arguing that the armed forces must be prepared so that no one interferes in the country.

World.title: Uruguay to open Pope Leo XIV's first South American tour
World.content:
Uruguay to open Pope Leo XIV's first South American tour

6th Thursday, August 2026 - 09:37 UTC Full article

The pontiff will remain in Uruguay from November 6 to 8, visiting Montevideo, Paysandú and Florida

Uruguay will be the first stop on Pope Leo XIV's apostolic journey to South America between November 6 and 17, the director of the Holy See Press Office, Matteo Bruni, confirmed on Wednesday.

The pontiff will remain in Uruguay from November 6 to 8, visiting Montevideo, Paysandú and Florida. He will continue to Argentina, where he will be from the 8th to the 11th in Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján, and conclude in Peru from the 11th to the 17th, with stops in Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa. That is ten cities in twelve days, the longest international trip of his pontificate, surpassing April's African tour. The Vatican said he accepted invitations from the heads of state and church authorities of the three countries, and that the detailed program will be released later.

According to unofficial information published by the Montevideo newspaper El País, the plan is for the pontiff to fly early on Saturday the 7th to Paysandú and, on returning to the capital, to visit the Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe church in the Borro neighborhood and tour Casavalle. A Mass would be held that evening at the Centenario Stadium, and on Sunday morning the Pope would be in Florida for the feast of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, the country's patron saint. The Holy See has not confirmed those details.

It will be the first papal visit to Uruguay in nearly four decades, after John Paul II's trips in 1987 and 1988. Uruguay has the lowest proportion of Catholics on the continent and a strictly secular state.

President Yamandú Orsi called the visit timely and a strong signal for the region. “South America appears as a region of peace. Of course, with our troubles: organized crime, all our problems, but this feels like a balm,” he said on the program Alguien tiene que decirlo.

Orsi also recounted that during his Vatican audience in October 2025, the Pope and his team had studied the parliamentary process behind Uruguay's euthanasia law and set out their views. “He is perfectly clear about who we are, our characteristics,” he said, adding that the exchange showed him the Vatican is a more significant center of political decision-making than is often assumed. Uruguay carried out its first legal euthanasia this year. The president also reflected on secularism, which he described as a distinctly Uruguayan debate, and called for firm tolerance toward all faiths.

In Argentina, presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier called the Pope's arrival a historic event and announced an interministerial team to coordinate logistics, security and protocol. The Argentine Catholic hierarchy has been critical of Javier Milei's economic policy over the past two years.

Argentina and Uruguay were not visited by Francis during his twelve-year pontificate; his last trip to the region was to Panama in January 2019. Peru had not received a pope since 2018. Robert Francis Prevost, born in Chicago in 1955 and holding Peruvian citizenship, served as a missionary there after his ordination in 1982 and led the Chiclayo diocese between 2015 and 2023. Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori said the country awaits him with open hearts.

World.title: An award-winning bakery launches a definitive ‘map’ of Mexico’s abundant bread types
World.content:
Building on Mexico News Daily’s history of Mexican bread, published earlier this year, two Mexican bakers have created a new “map” that charts the vast, often overlooked world of Mexican breads — from conchas and bolillos to coyotas, pan de muerto and rosca de Reyes.

The Primer Mapa del Pan Mexicano — or First Map of Mexican Bread — is a research project by siblings Ariana and Julio González, the founding bakers at 13-year-old Buñuelo in Naucalpan, State of México.

Instead of sorting breads by state or region, the map tracks their baking lineage: dough, technique and tradition.

That framework shows how one preparation style can develop into breads with markedly different shapes, textures and uses, with seemingly unrelated pieces sharing production methods or customs.

The map includes sweet breads, or pan dulce, savory staples and festive breads such as pan de muerto for Día de Muertos and rosca de Reyes for Three Kings Day.

The savory family includes bolillo, telera, pambazo, cemita and hojaldra, breads commonly used in tortas and other Mexican sandwiches.

Other families include bizcocho — sweet, cake-like breads including conchas, nubes and pelones — and the cookie family, which includes cochinitos de piloncillo, coricos and coyotas, the last being Sonoran pastries typically filled with piloncillo.

Other breads in the festive category include pan de pulque, pan de yema and a specialty bread sold at festivals and patron saint celebrations in Puebla and Tlaxcala called pan de fiesta or pan de feria.

The González siblings — recently named Bakers of the Year by the Mexico Gastronomic Guide — developed the project through years of fieldwork at traditional and contemporary bakeries. Designer Marcela Morales turned the research into a reference piece.

The total number of Mexican breads remains an elusive proposition. Estimates often put the figure above 1,000 varieties, but the map is not presented as a census. Its 52 selections are representative samples meant to illuminate a larger and still-changing baking heritage.

“This map is not intended to be a definitive catalog of Mexican breadmaking, but rather an invitation to see it from a different perspective,” Julio González said, “We want people to understand that behind each piece there are techniques, traditions, and baking families that are all part of the same heritage.”

The map arrives after a period of renewed attention to Mexican breadmaking.

In late 2025, a British baker based in Mexico City voiced a blunt opinion about Mexican breads culture (or, in his opinion, lack thereof) and received widespread backlash, including a Mexico News Daily piece noting, “You’re free to dislike bolillos … Just don’t use cultural superiority as a seasoning.”

Then earlier this year, Panadería Rosetta in Mexico City was named one of the world’s 10 best pastry makers by La Liste, a prestigious Paris‑based global dining guide.

For now, the single-sheet map is being sold for 135 pesos (US $7.88) at Buñuelo, Av. Alcanfores 44-2 in Naucalpan. See the bakery’s Instagram for more details, including a planned digital version.

With reports from Food & Wine en Español and El Universal

World.title: Opinion: The real reason San Miguel de Allende feels so American
World.content:
Since I arrived in San Miguel de Allende over six weeks ago for a nine-week journalism internship, I have been trying to figure out why more international tourists do not come to central Mexico.

I have written about my experiences across the Bajío cities of Guanajuato and Quereétaro as well as Mexico City. I have been constantly surprised by the lack of American tourists, or sometimes even tourists in general, in what I felt like were incredible destinations for a vacation.

But I have yet to write about the tourists in the place where I’ve been living. A place flooded with local and international tourists on weekends and a place where the economy revolves around visitors. San Miguel is seemingly the one place in the region where American tourists are around every corner. So what sets San Miguel apart? Why do Americans flock here instead of Guanajuato or Querétaro?

It all started nearly 80 years ago when the emergence of art schools in San Miguel allowed Americans to take classes abroad. This, in turn, brought new business and development, with hotels opening throughout the city. San Miguel’s famous colonial streets were declared a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2008, spurring more development and tourism.

Now San Miguel is widely regarded as one of the top international destinations in Mexico, bringing in over two million visitors each year. There are an abundance of vineyards just outside the city limits, fine dining is around every corner and luxury hotels are found all throughout town.

As more and more foreigners came to San Miguel and as the arts scene continued to grow, the town became increasingly accommodating to American tourists. Americans tend to like to feel comfortable abroad, and the prevalence of English in the town takes away a massive hurdle that might deter Americans from going to Guanajuato or Querétaro, where English is less prevalent.

More Americans also means more American food, more American sports on TV, and more spaces designed to make Americans feel comfortable. Jewish delis, burger joints and microbreweries covered with TVs are easy to find — and they are harder to come by in Guanajuato or Querétaro. More places for Americans will always lead to more Americans.

The invention of social media has also greatly benefited San Miguel’s tourism industry. The Parroquia de San Miguel Árcangel — with its towering spires and jaw-dropping pink facade — looks glorious in an Instagram story. The courtyards and gardens throughout the town also make for great photos, and some have called San Miguel’s local Starbucks the most beautiful in the world.

Once San Miguel was named the best city in the world by Travel and Leisure magazine, more visitors than ever began to arrive.

San Miguel is also small and relatively relaxed. It’s dense and walkable, to the point that residents do not need a car to get around. It has a large local bar scene, but not many clubs. The weather is consistent and relatively mild year-round. All of these — along with cheaper prices than the United States — have made San Miguel a picture-perfect place for American retirees looking for something different late in life. With retirees generally less motivated to learn Spanish, the influx of English-speakers forced business to cater to that demographic.

While San Miguel is definitely popular, it still is not widely known in the United States. When most Americans think of tourism in Mexico, they imagine the picturesque beaches of Cancún, Los Cabos or Puerto Vallarta. Mexico City is rapidly growing as an international tourist destination and those seeking more of an adventure have probably heard of Oaxaca. Despite the high volume of arrivals, San Miguel de Allende does not have the same level of international recognition as other Mexican destinations.

And it shouldn’t. San Miguel is a small city that has already been drastically gentrified. Homes throughout Centro have been replaced by shops and restaurants, the cost of living continues to climb, and there is a lack of jobs outside of the tourism industry.

So what sets San Miguel apart? It’s at the top of tourism rankings, while other beautiful Bajío towns receive less attention. It has splashes of Mexican culture while still feeling comfortable for Americans.

Does that make San Miguel better than other cities? Yes and no. It feels more Americanized, which makes it attractive to American tourists. But the vibe isn’t just American — it’s international. Expats mingle with locals, and travelers from all over the world visit the cobblestone streets. It’s a destination for a reason, but a lot of those reasons can be found in a lot of other cities in the region — without the crowds, or price tag, that have followed San Miguel’s fame.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Seaweed diplomacy: Mexico and Japan to tackle sargassum crisis in new joint program
World.content:
The Foreign Ministry has announced that Japan will be participating in the development of a joint program to address the massive influx of sargassum on Mexico’s shores.

Japan — which has been actively collaborating with Caribbean nations to tackle the sargassum problems plaguing the region — will offer ocean-monitoring technology, specialized equipment including robotics and sensors and financial cooperation.

Additionally, Japan will provide sargassum-collecting ships and vessels adapted for the collection of the macroalgae at sea in order to strengthen Mexico’s capacity to address the situation along its Caribbean beaches.

The collaboration will also feature satellite monitoring, biological decomposition technologies for sargassum and technical training programs through Japan’s International Cooperation Agency, in coordination with Mexico’s Agency for International Development Cooperation.

The project will include academic research, as well as business-oriented research and development. This work will focus on processes for converting the sargassum, as a raw material, into commercially viable products, such as fertilizer, biofuels, building materials and soap.

The goal is to boost marine and nearshore coastal conservation efforts, support integrated coastal management actions and mitigate negative impacts on sectors such as fisheries, public health and tourism.

The announcement came during an Aug. 3 meeting between Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco and his Japanese counterpart, Toshimitsu Motegi, in which they agreed to establish a working group to advance new areas of collaboration to strengthen bilateral relations in the political, economic, scientific and technological spheres.

In a joint statement to the media, they announced the launch of a high-level economic dialogue to boost bilateral trade, which, from January to May this year, amounted to US $9.9 billion, a 4% increase compared to the same period last year.

A few days earlier, President Claudia Sheinbaum pledged 2 billion pesos in federal funds (US $115 million) to battle an influx of sargassum in the state of Quintana Roo.

These funds will be directed toward sargassum control efforts spanning roughly 30 miles of beachfront spanning resorts including Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Puerto Morelos, Tulum and Mahahual.

El secretario de Relaciones Exteriores, Roberto Velasco (@r_velascoa), recibió a su homólogo japonés, el ministro de Asuntos Exteriores de @MofaJapan_en, Motegi Toshimitsu (@moteging), quien realiza una visita de trabajo a nuestro país. En reunión bilateral, ambos titulares de… pic.twitter.com/iaZwAhBjjV — Relaciones Exteriores (@SRE_mx) August 3, 2026

In October, Cancún will host the international EU-Caribbean Global Gateway Conference on Sargassum, with the aim of articulating joint strategies for the containment and management of biomass and sargassum.

The conference is expected to focus on regional cooperation, circular economy solutions and sargassum-harvesting technology.

With reports from Excelsior and MVS Noticias

World.title: The Mexican peso hits its strongest level against the dollar in 6 months
World.content:
Mexico’s currency gained 0.12% vs the U.S. dollar in Thursday trading, extending its rally to 10 straight days after the central bank left interest rates unchanged at its Aug. 6 monetary policy meeting.

The peso closed Thursday at 17.21 to the US dollar and dipped below 17.14 in early trading on Friday, an additional 0.58% gain and its strongest level against the U.S. dollar since Feb. 23.

Forbes México attributed Friday’s early action to a negative U.S. jobs report and said the peso is on pace to appreciate by 1.3% by the end of the week.

Mexico’s currency was also boosted by the central bank’s unanimous decision on Thursday to hold its benchmark rate at 6.50% for a second consecutive meeting, while hinting that rates would remain at the current level for the foreseeable future.

In a statement, Banxico’s board of governors said “headline and core inflation are expected to decline throughout the forecast horizon, albeit more gradually than previously anticipated.”

Headline inflation slowed in July for a fourth consecutive month though the central bank does not expect it to converge to its 3% target until late next year.

In a social media post, Gabriela Siller, director of analysis at Grupo Financerio BASE, said the peso is also appreciating “due to the carry-trade,” a strategy whereby an investor borrows money in a currency with a low interest rate and invests those funds into higher-yielding assets or currencies.

Siller said large global investors are borrowing in the U.S. and Japan, then investing in Mexico, indicating that the peso continues to benefit from a wide interest rate differential (Mexico’s 6.50% policy rate compares favorably to the U.S. Federal Reserve’s 3.50%-3.75% target range).

The newspaper El Economista said the U.S. jobs report (which noted that U.S. nonfarm payrolls fell by 23,000 jobs last month, following a downwardly revised increase of 20,000 jobs the previous month) prompted the market to reduce bets that U.S. interest rates will rise.

Monex Grupo Financiero concurred, saying in a statement that the peso’s advance against the dollar is “driven by the weakness of the dollar and a readjustment of expectations on the direction of the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy” at its next meeting in September.

With reports from El Economista and Forbes México

World.title: After crushing Panama, Mexico’s Under-20 team looks to clinch Olympics berth
World.content:
Close on the heels of El Tri’s impressive World Cup performance, Mexico’s Under-20 men’s squad has qualified for next year’s U-20 World Cup and is on the verge of earning an invitation to the 2028 Olympics.

At the same time, El Tri’s U-23 team has reached the final of the Central America and Caribbean Games where it will face Venezuela on Friday evening in Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic.

México vs Panamá | 2026 Concacaf Men's Under-20 Championship Quarterfinals

Watch this video on YouTube

Coach Alex Diego’s U-20 team faces Canada on Friday night in Puebla with a spot in the final on the line. The winner will face either Costa Rica or Team USA who play earlier Friday.

Team Mexico earned its berth in the semifinals by manhandling Panama 4-0 on Wednesday, its fourth straight shut-out in the tournament, which features 12 teams from the Concacaf region competing for four tickets to the World Cup.

All four semifinalists automatically secured invites to the U-20 World Cup, so now the battle is for the lone remaining Concacaf berth in the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

As the host nation, the U.S. receives one of the two Olympics spots reserved for Concacaf teams.

That means if Team USA defeats Costa Rica and Mexico gets past Canada, El Mini Tri will have clinched a trip to the Olympics regardless of the outcome in Sunday’s final. However, if Costa Rica upsets the Stars-and-Stripes, then Mexico would have to win the final to earn a spot in the Olympics.

Of course, coach Diego’s goal is to hoist the trophy on home soil, but to do so, El Tri will have to overcome a pair of key injuries and the suspension of its first-choice goalie.

Attacking midfielder Santiago Sandoval required surgery after breaking a finger during the team’s 2-0 victory over Costa Rica in the team’s second group stage match, ending his participation in the tournament.

Of equal concern is the status of winger Hugo Camberos, a rising star who has attracted attention from English Premier League clubs.

Camberos has scored in each of Mexico’s matches thus far, but limped off the pitch late in Wednesday’s match and his availability for the semifinal is in question.

The situation in goal for Mexico is of lesser concern since back-up goalie Cristo Navarrete kept a clean sheet in both starts since first-choice keeper Juan Liceaga was shown a red card in El Tri’s second match.

With reports from ESPN, FIFA, N+ and Concacaf

World.title: Meet the woman bringing adobe back to a Maya village
World.content:
Recently, on a trip to Valladolid, I met a woman named Debi Morris, who is bringing adobe back to the Maya village of Ek’ Balam by building a community center out of the all-natural, sustainable material.

Morris fell in love with Ek’ Balam years ago after a taxi dropped her off in the middle of town rather than at the Ek’ Balam ruins. She was captivated by the warm, welcoming people, the laughing children and the surrounding smiles. So she decided to give back using adobe.

What is adobe?

Adobe is a highly durable, all-natural building material that, with proper maintenance and moisture protection, can last for centuries. The proof is still standing in Yotzil, a tiny village in Yucatán. Other historic structures, such as New Mexico’s Palace of the Governors, built in 1610, still stand strong, proving adobe’s longevity.

Made of locally sourced natural materials, adobe recipes vary slightly from place to place depending on the soil and sand. In Ek’ Balam, it is made of high-clay red dirt, sand, dried grass, agave fiber, water and horse manure. Dried beforehand, the manure carries no odor. Builders also added a layer of fermented cactus juice, called baba de nopal, to waterproof the exterior walls.

Adobe also offers high thermal mass, making it ideal for escaping the heat of a Yucatán summer. Because of this thermal efficiency, adobe is growing in popularity as people look for ways to adapt to rising temperatures and reduce air conditioning usage.

Key characteristics of adobe

Composition: Typically consists of blended clay, sand, silt, a fibrous binder (such as chopped straw or agave fibers) and water to bind the mixture and prevent cracking.

Thermal mass: Thick adobe walls absorb heat during the day and slowly release it at night, providing natural climate control in hot, arid environments.

Sustainability: Sourced directly from the earth, adobe is non-toxic, biodegradable and fully recyclable.

Durability: Traditional adobe lasts for centuries but remains susceptible to water erosion, and so requires regular maintenance.

Adapting adobe to local soil

“You’re going to need patience. This is trial and error. There is no specific formula,” an expert advised Morris when she began.

She learned through trial and error that everything depends on local materials. For example, a builder cannot use the same formula in Mérida, even though it is in the same state of Yucatán, because the soil composition differs. In Ek’ Balam, one plot may have red dirt, while a neighboring plot contains entirely different mineral compounds.

“That was an eye-opener,” Morris said.

Not all red dirt works; the clay content must be tested first. “Thank God ours did, so that was a big blessing,” she said. Each layer requires experimentation.

Building in Ek’ Balam

Construction begins with the frame: two layers of wood with a layer of rock in between. Once the frame is set, builders apply the first layer of adobe — a mixture of red dirt, water and dried zacate, a local grass found in surrounding fields. The mixture is combined using hands and feet.

Next comes the layering process: rock, adobe, rock, adobe. After drying for two days, the structure is ready for a second layer consisting of red dirt, sand, water and dried grass. For this layer, the grass is treated with borax to repel insects.

The third layer contains red dirt, fine double-sifted sand, sifted horse manure and agave fibers, which are also treated with borax and cut into 1- to 2-centimeter pieces.

Finally, builders add baba de nopal, or prickly pear cactus extract. The extract is made by removing spines from cactus paddles, chopping them and fermenting them in water for at least 24 hours before straining.

Once the third layer is completed, it is sprayed with water several times a day for five days to retain moisture. On the eighth day, smoothed cracks are treated with warmed cactus extract for waterproofing. Before hurricane season, a final layer of natural linseed oil is applied for additional weather protection without compromising thermal performance.

Reviving an ancient practice

In 2004, Ek’ Balam consisted primarily of traditional palapas. Today, concrete homes have become common, but they trap heat, leading residents to joke that they feel like pizza ovens. Adobe offers a solution rooted in local heritage.

Although adobe construction was an ancient Maya technique, the knowledge was lost generations ago. Morris visited several villages asking abuelitos (grandfathers) if they knew how to make adobe. The answer was almost always, “My grandfather did.” In one nearby village, centuries-old adobe walls are still standing, proving the material’s regional durability.

As a result, Ek’ Balam has welcomed the return of this traditional building method.

Mexico Correspondent for International Living, Bel is an experienced writer, author, photographer and videographer with 500+ articles published both in print and across digital platforms. Living in the Mexican Caribbean for over seven years now, she’s in love with Mexico and has no plans to go anywhere anytime soon.

World.title: Estadio Azteca owners lost an estimated $47M on FIFA’s most profitable World Cup ever
World.content:
Grupo Ollamani, which owns the iconic Estadio Azteca, is perhaps one of the big financial losers of the World Cup after the release of a new financial report, cited by El País, that reveals a multi-million dollar loss.

The holding company, which also owns the publishing subsidiary of Grupo Televisa, reported to the Mexican Stock Exchange (BMV) a net loss of 557.2 million pesos (US $32.2 million) in its second-quarter financial results, primarily associated with the cost of the World Cup.

Led by media mogul Emilio Azcárraga Jean, Grupo Ollamani also estimated an additional financial impact of 255.9 million pesos (US $14.9 million) in July, when the stadium also hosted World Cup matches.

Combined, the total impact would amount to 813 million pesos (US $47.4 million) covering the costs of what’s been described as FIFA operations.

These operations include making Estadio Azteca (also known as Estadio Banorte) available to host five matches and organizing tournament-related activities in Mexico City.

Cause of losses

Ollamani said the reported financial loss was partly due to payments related to a dispute over the use of the stadium’s premium seats and box seats.

In the lead-up to the event, people who owned boxes and premium seats inside the stadium demanded those seats for World Cup matches. But FIFA ultimately required full control. A legal dispute was eventually resolved, whereby Ollamani had to pay FIFA 1 billion pesos (US $58.3 million) so the owners could use their seats.

The company noted that the negative financial impact did not reflect the ordinary course of its operations and stems from extraordinary circumstances related to the World Cup.

“At the same time, investments were made to prepare and modernize Banorte Stadium — representing long-term improvements to its infrastructure, functionality, operational capacity, and digitalization — the benefits of which will extend beyond the World Cup period,” the company said in a statement cited by El País.

Ollamani’s report adds to a broader picture that confirms the World Cup did not generate the expected economic impact. The results were particularly disappointing for the hospitality sector.

In stark contrast, FIFA emerged as the tournament’s biggest financial winner, reportedly generating a record US $15 billion in revenue, which far exceeded its US $11 billion forecast. This performance was mainly fueled by the sale of licensing, broadcasting and hospitality rights, as well as sponsorships and ticketing sales.

With reports from El País, The Guardian and Infobae

World.title: Mexico reestablishes diplomatic relations with Peru: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📉 Inflation falls to 3.12%: Sheinbaum highlighted INEGI data showing headline inflation dropped to 3.12% in July from 3.37% in June, calling the decline “very important.” It’s the lowest rate since May 2020.

Sheinbaum highlighted INEGI data showing headline inflation dropped to 3.12% in July from 3.37% in June, calling the decline “very important.” It’s the lowest rate since May 2020. ✈️ Bettsy Chávez arrives in Mexico: Sheinbaum announced former Peruvian PM Bettsy Chávez was “about to land” in Mexico, after months of asylum at Mexico’s Lima embassy under Brazil’s protection following Peru’s diplomatic break with Mexico last November.

Sheinbaum announced former Peruvian PM Bettsy Chávez was “about to land” in Mexico, after months of asylum at Mexico’s Lima embassy under Brazil’s protection following Peru’s diplomatic break with Mexico last November. 🇲🇽 🇵🇪 Mexico and Peru to restore relations: Sheinbaum said President Keiko Fujimori’s new government granted Chávez safe passage as a “good will” gesture, and announced Mexico and Peru would reestablish diplomatic ties. She reaffirmed support for ousted ex-President Castillo.

Sheinbaum said President Keiko Fujimori’s new government granted Chávez safe passage as a “good will” gesture, and announced Mexico and Peru would reestablish diplomatic ties. She reaffirmed support for ousted ex-President Castillo. ⚖️ Ex-Guerrero governor’s arrest “not political”: Asked about Thursday’s arrest of Ángel Aguirre over alleged concealment of Ayotzinapa-related video evidence, Sheinbaum denied any political motive.

Asked about Thursday’s arrest of Ángel Aguirre over alleged concealment of Ayotzinapa-related video evidence, Sheinbaum denied any political motive. 🚫 No fracking in Tampico-Misantla basin: Sheinbaum reaffirmed her government would follow the expert committee’s recommendation against fracking there, citing Indigenous peoples, rich biodiversity and serious potential environmental impacts.

Sheinbaum reaffirmed her government would follow the expert committee’s recommendation against fracking there, citing Indigenous peoples, rich biodiversity and serious potential environmental impacts. 🥑 Officials to discuss avocado certification suspension: Sheinbaum said Mexican officials would meet U.S. Embassy representatives Friday morning to address security concerns behind the suspension, aiming to resume Michoacán avocado exports. Why today’s mañanera matters

Today’s mañanera was important as President Claudia Sheinbaum spoke about a wide range of significant topics.

They included inflation, diplomatic relations with Peru, the arrest of a former governor, fracking and the suspension of U.S. avocado certifications in Michoacán.

Sheinbaum acknowledges decline in inflation

At the very start of her press conference, Sheinbaum highlighted that Mexico’s headline inflation rate fell to 3.12% in July, per data published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Friday.

She noted that the headline rate fell to that level from 3.37% in June, and described the decline as “very important.”

The inflation rate in July — just above the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target — was the lowest rate since May 2020.

Sheinbaum announces arrival of Bettsy Chávez to Mexico

Sheinbaum told reporters that former Peruvian Prime Minister Bettsy Chávez was “about to land in Mexico.”

She noted that Chávez, who briefly served as prime minister during the presidency of Pedro Castillo, stayed in Mexico’s Embassy in Peru for several months. Last November, the government of Peru severed diplomatic relations with Mexico after Chávez, who was accused of rebellion, was granted asylum at the Mexican Embassy in Lima.

“This embassy had to close because Peru broke off relations with Mexico and she remained [in the embassy] under the protection of Brazil, to whom we are very grateful,” Sheinbaum said.
