The president said that Chávez was granted “safe passage” to travel to Mexico by the new Peruvian government, led by President Keiko Fujimori. She said that a Mexican Air Force plane traveled to the South American country to collect the ex-prime minister and bring her to Mexico.

Sheinbaum: Mexico and Peru to reestablish relations

Sheinbaum said that the granting of safe passage to Chávez was an act of “good will” from the government of President Fujimori “toward Mexico.”

She subsequently announced that Mexico and Peru would reestablish diplomatic relations.

“I don’t know if I can announce it now or not, but I’m going to announce it. With this [act of good will], relations with Peru are going to be reestablished,” Sheinbaum said.

“And we, as always, as we have done, are going to continue defending President Castillo,” said Sheinbaum, who last September described the 2022 ousting of the ex-president by the Peruvian Congress as a “coup.”

“… The new government of Peru knows that,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Arrest of ex-governor of Guerrero has nothing to do with politics

A reporter asked the president about the arrest on Thursday of former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre, who is alleged to have ordered the concealment of security camera video footage that showed the bus on which students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers College were traveling at the time it was stopped by police in Iguala, Guerrero, on Sept. 26, 2014. Forty-three students were abducted and presumably murdered after the bus was stopped.

Sheinbaum said that the arrest of Aguirre — governor of Guerrero between 2011 and 2014 — was the result of months of work by the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR). She said that the FGR has adopted “new ways of investigating” the Ayotzinapa case.

“It may be the same evidence, but now they’re deepening [the investigation] through different mechanisms, many of which involve scientific analysis,” Sheinbaum said.

Asked whether the arrest of Aguirre had a “political background,” the president responded: “It has nothing to do with a political issue. It’s part of an investigation.”

As governor, Aguirre represented the Democratic Revolution Party, or PRD, but he was previously affiliated with the Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, for decades. Mexico’s president at the time of the students’ disappearance was Enrique Peña Nieto, who represented the PRI both as president between 2012 and 2018 and governor of México state between 2005 and 2011.

Sheinbaum explains why there will be no fracking in the Tampico-Misantla basin

Sheinbaum reiterated that no final decision has been taken regarding the commencement of large-scale fracking in two shale basins in northern Mexico.

Subsequently, a day after an expert fracking committee publicly announced its recommendation against fracking in the resource-rich Tampico-Misantla basin in Veracruz and Tamaulipas, the president reaffirmed that her government would heed that advice.

“In the Tampico-Misantla basin, [there will be] no [fracking] there,” Sheinbaum said.

“Why? Because there are Indigenous peoples, because the nature is very rich, because the environmental impacts would be very serious,” she said.

Despite those remarks, Sheinbaum has asserted that the use of “new technologies” can make fracking a sustainable practice that doesn’t harm the environment.

Mexican and US officials to discuss suspension of avocado certifications

Sheinbaum told reporters that Mexican officials would meet with U.S. Embassy officials on Friday morning to discuss the U.S. government’s suspension of avocado certifications in Michoacán due to security concerns.

She said that the “objective” of today’s meeting is to address the U.S. government’s concerns with a view to resuming avocado exports to the United States.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Department of the Environment provides update on Fish Kill in the Belize River Valley area
World.content:
Department of the Environment provides update on Fish Kill in the Belize River Valley area

INVESTIGATION INTO THE FISH KILL IN THE BELIZE RIVER VALLEY AREA

Belmopan, Belize. August 7, 2026: The public is hereby informed that, as part of the ongoing investigation into the fish kill in the Belize River Valley area, the Department of the Environment (DOE) has conducted visual observations and water quality assessments from near Banana Bank, upstream of Santander Farms, to the Burrell Boom Village bridge. Significant fish mortality and changes in water conditions were observed particularly along the approximately 17.5-mile stretch between Isabella Bank and Grace Bank. The Department is also assessing discharge points and other activities along and within the vicinity of the river as part of its investigation into the possible source or sources of the event.

On-site water quality testing and sampling have been conducted at various locations along the river. Preliminary field results recorded extremely low levels of dissolved oxygen in areas where significant fish mortality was observed, together with elevated conductivity, chlorophyll-a and turbidity at certain locations. These conditions can adversely affect aquatic life. Samples have been submitted for laboratory analysis to assist in determining the cause of the observed conditions.

As part of the ongoing investigation, the DOE has also collected water samples from the Santander Farms drainage system and at locations downstream for chemical analysis. Fish and sediment samples are also being collected and analysed to assist in determining the cause of the fish mortality and whether contaminants may have contributed to the event.

The Department is additionally reviewing satellite imagery from before and during the event to assess changes in water conditions, land-clearing activities and other factors that may assist in identifying potential contributing sources. Investigations and assessments are also being conducted in relation to other developments, activities and potential discharge points within the wider area.

At this stage, the Department has not determined the source or responsible party associated with the fish kill. The investigation remains ongoing, and any determination will be based on the results of laboratory analyses and the totality of the scientific and technical evidence collected.

The precautionary advisory issued by the Department on August 5, 2026, remains in effect. The public is therefore advised not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from the affected areas and not to use untreated river water for drinking, cooking, food preparation, livestock or pets until further notice. This advisory applies to untreated water taken directly from the river and does not apply to treated potable water supplied by Belize Water Services Limited.

The DOE continues to coordinate with relevant government agencies and other authorities in monitoring the situation and advancing the investigation. The public will be informed as laboratory results and other verified findings become available.

The Department of the Environment remains committed to protecting Belize’s environment, safeguarding our natural resources and public health, and ensuring that all potential sources are thoroughly investigated and that appropriate action is taken where the evidence establishes a breach of Belize’s environmental laws.

END

World.title: Election Season Starts – Poll of UDP convention in the Culture Capital this weekend
World.content:
Election Season Starts – Poll of UDP convention in the Culture Capital this weekend

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News

By Dr. Philip Castillo: Municipal elections are eight months away and the first steps start with party conventions to select Mayoral and councilor candidates. The Opposition UDP will hold its convention this weekend on August 9. The convention will feature two candidates vying for Mayor, and each candidate has his/her respective slate of six councilor candidates. Hence the ballot will have a total of 14 candidates. Only 7 can win.

Castillo Poll # 3 of 2026 presents the findings of a poll conducted in Dangriga over the weekend of August 1st to 3rd. For a municipal election, the target population is the registered voters of that municipality. However for a party convention, that target population deliberately excludes known members of the other party. So for the upcoming UDP convention, the party will not allow known PUP members to vote. That presents a major challenge since ascertaining who is a “known PUP” is a subjective endeavour. This also means that for polling purposes, the actual target population is unknown.

The above, notwithstanding…here goes:

Table 1 – Mayor

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

Table 2 – Councilors

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

A poll is a sample randomly drawn from a given population. I’ve already noted the challenges of identifying the target population. Yet another challenge undertaking any poll is that there WILL always be a margin of error. The margin of error relates to the extent to which the mean or the average of the sample (which is known) varies from the mean or the parameter of wider population (which is unknown). This degree of variance is expressed as a plus (+) or minus (-) because the variation can go in either direction. Polling organizations generally use a margin of error of +/- 3 percentage points. This poll had a margin of error of +/- 9%.

Another statistic that must be noted is the degree of confidence. This refers to the extent to which if you draw repeat samples you realistically expect the same results. For this poll the degree of confidence was at 90 %. This means that if the sample was drawn a hundred times, in ninety out of those one hundred times, the expected result would be the very same. Polling organizations generally use a degree of confidence of 95%.

From my projections, I estimate the voting population on Sunday August 9th 2026 to be around 695 voters. However accounting for the margin of error, the voting population could be as low as 9% less than 695. Or as high as 9% above 695. The actual ranges are 633 to 757 .

Tables 1 and 2 above are redone using these numbers to estimate actual votes.

Table 3 – Mayor

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

Table 4 – Councilors

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

Accounting for the margin of error, Dayton Sabal, Jamall Swaso and John Sabal are still EXPECTED to win. Elsworth Magdaleno and Albourne Mashall are LIKELY to win. For the sixth and final council seat, probabilistically and because the numbers fall within the range of the margin of error, Marsha Mejia and Cindy Fajardo are favorites BUT Steven Laurie and Francis Marin have a punchers chance.

Dr. Philip Castillo is a development economist and an independent pollster. Send comments to [email protected].

World.title: Santander responds to Belize River fish kill, says factory does not routinely discharge process water into river
World.content:
Santander responds to Belize River fish kill, says factory does not routinely discharge process water into river

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Santander Sugar Group (SSG) has issued a statement amid concerns over the recent loss of aquatic life in the Belize River Valley, saying it is cooperating fully with an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Environment (DoE) and other government agencies.

In a statement issued Friday, August 7, Santander said it is “deeply saddened” by the reported loss of aquatic life and has granted authorities unrestricted access to its facilities and operations. The company did not accept responsibility for the fish kill, and said it welcomes the completion of the government’s investigation.

Santander said its processing facility operates as a closed-loop system in which process water is recovered, cooled where necessary and reused. According to the company, there is no continuous process effluent stream or routine discharge of high-temperature process water from its factory into the Belize River.

The company also stressed that its canals are not connected to Labouring Creek and said its operations account for approximately 12 percent of the agricultural land within the broader watershed.

Santander has faced environmental scrutiny in the past. In 2012, the company’s development was linked to the dredging of a large canal through the Labouring Creek Jaguar Corridor Wildlife Sanctuary, and in 2016 government authorities cited Santander for breaches of its Environmental Compliance Plan following investigations into activities affecting environmentally sensitive areas.

The present investigation, however, remains ongoing, and authorities have not publicly established that Santander caused the reported aquatic deaths. Santander says it will review any findings and recommendations issued by regulators and remains committed to environmental compliance and protection of the Belize River watershed.

World.title: Surviving burn victims from Guardsman fire return home
World.content:
Fabian Brown, one of the two surviving men of four initially injured in a fire returns home after treatment in the US alongside his wife Myeisha (out of frame)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Two of the four men injured in an explosion at a garage adjacent to Guardsman Group-Beryllium Limited headquarters, on South Camp Road, have returned to Jamaica following intensive burn treatment overseas.

Fabian Brown was one of two airlifted back to Jamaica on Friday in the company of his wife, Myesha, who spoke to Observer Online.

“The journey, I must say, has been rough. It has been hard,” she said.

Despite this, Myesha had high praise for those involved in her husband’s care, including the staff of Wellstar Cobb Burn Centre and Trinity Airlines as well as the Burn Foundation of Jamaica and their Crisis Support Charity arm.

She issued an urgent call to corporate Jamaica to put their support behind the foundation.

“I encourage Jamaica, corporate Jamaica, to support the Crisis Support Charity…it’s not just supporting the survivors. It’s not just burned people alone. But overall, if you look at what they have done, they’ve been doing good. And if it wasn’t for them, we would not have been able to leave here and for him to get that thorough care that he needs.”

Guardsman had committed to supporting the men who were injured in the May 27 incident, which firefighters said happened before 9:00 am while welding work was being done on the property.

Brown was airlifted along with Damian Walters and a third man for care overseas after the incident. The fourth man passed away at a local hospital before he could be airlifted. Walters also passed away while undergoing treatment overseas.

READ: Employee injured in Guardsman fire succumbs to injuries

Meanwhile, as Myesha expressed her sorrow at the two deaths, she and Fabian are now preparing for a life that may look significantly different.

“The journey is just beginning. People might think, oh, you get burned, you’re healed. This is a life-changing experience. People need to understand that when you experience burns and you’re recovering, it takes years, and your life will never be the same. The sun, something that we take for granted, you can no longer go in that,” she said.

Despite the challenges, she expressed faith in God and gratitude for her husband’s life.

“Not until you have someone who has been affected severely by burns can you know what that journey is, and I’m thankful, grateful that Fabian is still here with us,” she said.

World.title: 3-year-old dies in suspected drowning in Westmoreland
World.content:
WESTMORELAND, Jamaica — Westmoreland police are investigating a suspected drowning following the death of a three-year-old child at a popular attraction in Little Bay, Westmoreland, on Independence Day.

The deceased has been identified as Kayson Barrett of an Ocean Pointe address in the parish of Hanover.

Reports from the police indicate that around 2:45 pm, the child, his mother, and another relative were at the attraction when he reportedly wandered away unnoticed, prompting his parent and the relative to launch a search.

Barrett was later found in a swimming pool on the property and taken to the lifeguard on duty, who immediately attempted to administer cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

The police were unable to say if any charges are pending.

World.title: Card, Douglas win silver in 100m at World U20 Championships
World.content:
Jamaica's Shanoya Douglas parades with the Jamaican flag after winning the silver medal in the women's 100m on Thursday's second day of the 2026 World Athletics Under 20 championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. Douglas, the world leader was beaten by American Maria Maxwell. (Photos: Paul Reid)

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s Gary Card and Shanoya Douglas won silver medals in the men and women’s 100m on Thursday night at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon.

It was the first medals for Jamaica at the championships, putting them in ninth position on the medals tables.

Americans Tate Taylor and Mia Maxwell delighted the home fans by winning the double, only the second time athletes from the same country had taken both gold medals at the same under-20 championships after Americans Noah Lyles and Candace Hill achieved the feat in 2016 in Bydgoszcz, Poland.

Card got off to a fast start but was chased and caught by Tate who passed him to win in a personal best 9.94 seconds (0.1m/s), the Jamaican second in 10.05 seconds. South Africa’s Marko Ferreira took the bronze with 10.16 seconds.

Maxwell got the edge over Douglas at the start and held off the Jamaican to the tape, running 11.14 seconds (-0.1m/s). Douglas finished second in 11.17 seconds with Italy’s Kelly Ann Maevane Doualla Edimo third in 11.27 seconds. Theianna-Lee Terrelonge was sixth in 11.37 seconds

It was the first time in 10 years an American won the women’s 100m and snapped the four-championships winning streak by the Jamaicans – Briana Williams in 2018, Tina Clayton in 2021 and 2022 and Alana Reid in 2024.

Also on Thursday, thrower Able Mills failed to record a legal throw in both the women’s discus and shot put finals that were held within two hours of each other.

Mills had thrown distances close to her lifetime bests to qualify for both finals but failed to make a legal mark in either.

Jamaica also failed to qualify any runner in the 400m finals set for Friday afternoon, all four failing to get past their semifinals.

Jabari Matheson who was running his fourth 400m race in two days, placed sixth in his semi-final in 47.29 seconds, the first time he failed to go under the 47.00 second mark at the championships.

Jason Pitter failed to get up to his high standards, and was sixth in his semi-final in 46.50 seconds after he advanced on time from the first round.

Daniellia Dixon was fifth in her semi-final in 53.77 seconds and Shameika McLean, who had run three times since the start of the championships, just failed to get into the final after placing fourth in her semis in 54.24 seconds.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Fingers crossed for ganja
World.content:
Walter Melbourne, director of licensing and applications at the Cannabis Licensing Authority, speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

THERE is no indication when Jamaica could see its first cannabis company registered on the local stock market, but key players in the sector are hopeful it will happen soon.

As global powers equivocate with the classification of the weed, leaders at Jamaica’s Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) are keeping their fingers crossed that the tight hold on the plant will be relaxed to allow the medical and commercial industry to grow.

During this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange the top brass of the CLA pointed to the recent indication by the United States (US) that cannabis could be moved from a Schedule I drug to Schedule III.

That announcement earlier this year was welcomed by players in the industry; however, months later it is not clear where cannabis will sit on the US drug scheduling list as US lawmakers continue debate on the matter.

According to CLA Chief Executive Officer Farrah Blake, “rescheduling of ganja would answer a lot of questions” in relation to access to the banking system and eligibility for grants for farmers and businesses in the industry.

As it relates to Jamaica possibly seeing its first regulated marijuana company hit the stock market, chair of the CLA Dr Nadeen Spence said, “We have to keep our fingers crossed” that marijuana will in fact be reclassified to reflect a Schedule III status.

It would, she argued, “translate into something that reassures the banking sector that ganja is not as risky as it currently is”.

Although uncertainty looms over ganja’s position on the list, Walter Melbourne, director of licensing and applications at the CLA, said there nevertheless needs to be an appreciation for the progress being achieved by the entity.

“Wherever we are now, it is a metamorphosis, a giant leap. In the 1970s, if you were caught with even a small amount it was a mandatory prison sentence. Some of our prominent people in society have had trouble. There was a lot of persecution and prosecution. Where we are now is really a massive step. I am making the point to say, who knows. Let’s keep going and we might very well see it there one day,” said Melbourne.

The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) describes Schedule I drugs as substances or chemicals with no currently accepted medical use and have a high potential for abuse, such as heroin and ecstasy.

Schedule III drugs are substances or chemicals with a moderate to low potential for physical and psychological dependence. The DEA states that drugs listed under Schedule III are considered to have less potential to be abused than Schedule I and II drugs.

The US Department of Justice has already officially reclassified cannabis as less dangerous, marking a major shift in that country’s drug policy.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche changed the classifications of products containing marijuana that are covered by the Food and Drug Administration or that have received a state medical marijuana licence.

They will move cannabis from a Schedule I narcotic like heroin to a Schedule III drug — on par with Tylenol with codeine.

Marijuana remains illegal at the federal level. Despite the federal ban, most US states have legalised the medical or recreational use of marijuana, and many have shops where it can be purchased legally.

World.title: Come Alive delivers!
World.content:
H.U.M.B.L.E (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

The East Lawns of King’s House became more than a venue on Saturday night. For several hours it was transformed by a sea of worshippers into a space of praise.

It was the perfect start to the month in which Jamaica celebrates its 64th year of Independence as hundreds gathered for the second staging of the Come Alive Gospel concert.

Dubbed a national call to worship, it became evident from the very first note that this was no ordinary musical showcase. It was an invitation — one that patrons answered with lifted hands, tear-filled eyes, and hearts fully surrendered to praise.

Christian worship, often confined to church walls, spilled freely across the grounds as saints gave their whole beings to the moment, proving that praise can command the same passion and intensity as any secular spectacle.

Yet, unlike the fleeting excitement of entertainment, what unfolded at King’s House was rooted in something deeper — an encounter with the divine.

The group H.U.M.B.L.E opened the main event with a spirited rendition of the Jamaican National Anthem, their harmonies echoing across the venue before they returned with a medley of old-time gospel favourites that ignited a revival spirit which lingered for the remainder of the programme.

That spirit only intensified when Petra Kaye took the stage. With a commanding voice that carried effortlessly across the lawns, the singer brought a fervency reminiscent of the “old-time religion” of generations past. Songs such as Crown Him, I Can Recommend My God, and the beloved Sovereign God Medley became more than performances. Attendees sang along with conviction, their praises rising heavenward like incense.

Johnmark Wiggan followed with a deeply personal set, sharing snippets of a testimony marked by trials that, by his own admission, should have destroyed him had it not been for the hand of God. As he delivered songs including Still Deh Yah, Because You Are Good, Run Me Dung, and Testimony, an intimate atmosphere settled over the audience. Eyes closed, hands lifted, and voices trembling with emotion, patrons appeared to journey back to defining moments in their Christian walk, as if remembering prayers answered, valleys crossed, and the faithfulness of God through every season.

The praise continued with Jermaine Edwards, whose set list included Peace In My Soul, Not Forget, Naa Bow, and Make You Smile. By the time he closed with his hit single Beautiful Day, the East Lawns had erupted into celebration.

Joy radiated from faces of attendance across the venue and, for a while, worries seemed to dissolve beneath the weight of worship.

Then came the evening’s international headliner, Michael W Smith.

Making a grand entrance, the singer’s band set the tone with a dramatic prelude before the legendary worship leader greeted the crowd.

“Jamaica, it’s so good to be here,” he said to great applause.

“We have a set list, but we might not stick to it,” he added, signalling that while plans had been made, the direction of the evening ultimately belonged to God.

Without hesitation, Smith launched into crowd favourites Open The Eyes of My Heart and Draw Me Close To You. The response was immediate. Worshippers surrendered themselves to the music.

Pausing between songs, Smith reflected on the immeasurable love of God; a love, he reminded the audience, that surpasses human understanding despite the Creator’s infinite power. He then transitioned into

Arms Around the Sun, a moving reminder of God’s unwavering affection for humanity.

Reflecting on his time in Jamaica, the singer shared that beyond the island’s beauty, it was the warmth and spirit of its people that had touched him most.

“Honestly, I love the people. I love your country, and I bless your country with all the promises of God,” he said before delivering favourites such as The Air I Breathe, Lord, I Give You My Heart, Above All, and There Is None Like You.

“Here is my prayer for Jamaica — at least one of them,” he said before leading the audience into

Let It Rain.

His set also included stirring renditions of Waymaker, Agnus Dei (Worthy Is The Lamb), Goodness of God, and Awesome God.

Had the curtains closed at that very moment, patrons would likely have left fulfilled, their faces glowing from an evening already overflowing with worship. But Come Alive still had one final offering.

Papa San emerged to deafening cheers, lifting the energy to even greater heights.

From the opening notes of Glory God, the veteran deejay had the audience captivated.

Songs like Hell Bruk Loose and Step Pan Di Enemy transformed the East Lawns into a grand dance floor as patrons abandoned their seats, dancing and rejoicing with uninhibited praise.

“I haven’t been here in a while ennu, so mek we go down memory lane likkle bit,” he told the crowd before launching into a nostalgic rendition of

Pop Style.

But amid the excitement, his message remained clear: “Worship should be a part of your life. Sing about what Jesus did for you,” he encouraged before performing Smile Again, a testimony of redemption and restoration.

Long after the final song faded, the message of the evening remained.

According to Eric Hosin, chairman of the Come Alive Collective, the success of the event was possible only because of God’s grace.

“We’re happy and giving God thanks and all the praises because this was only because of his goodness and his mercy,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“People seemed to have enjoyed themselves. Papa San closing was just something else, and we’re giving God thanks. We saw worship taking place with Michael W Smith, Jermaine Edwards, Johnmark Wiggan, Petra Kaye, and H.U.M.B.L.E, who started out with that lovely rendition of the national anthem. It was an amazing night.”

He added: “It was a national call to worship. We answered a call from the Lord, where He said He was seeking true worshippers. Persons even came with their tambourines for worship and we thank the Lord.”

World.title: FLOW’S US$25-M REBUILD
World.content:
Flow Jamaica has spent more than US$25 million on the Hurricane Melissa rebuild efforts. .

FLOW Jamaica has spent more than US$25 million ($3.90 billion) restoring its network after Hurricane Melissa, including US$12 million ($1.87 billion) during the second quarter as it continued reconnecting fixed-line customers in western Jamaica.

Balan Nair, chief executive officer of Liberty Latin America Limited (LILA), disclosed the expenditure during the company’s earnings call on Thursday, while discussing recovery work in Jamaica.

“The actual business operations itself is improving, and we are getting very close to getting back to full strength. As a matter of fact, our mobile business has improved coming out of this, and our market share has improved coming out of this. Our ARPU (average revenue per user) has improved coming out of this,” Nair said of the recovery effort.

Liberty’s Caribbean segment added 11,000 postpaid subscribers during the second quarter ended June 30, with 6,000 subscribers coming from the Jamaican market. Revenue from Jamaica was down US$3.1 million or three per cent to US$101.6 million ($15.86 billion) for the second quarter. Liberty’s quarterly filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission noted that Hurricane Melissa had a negative impact of US$8 million on revenue.

“We continue to see negative headwinds from Hurricane Melissa in Jamaica, the effect is clearly diminishing,” Nair said.

However, the recovery in Jamaica continues to be impacted by the pace of infrastructure restoration in western Jamaica. LILA noted that approximately 38,000 RGUs (revenue generating units) in the Jamaican market remained offline at the end of the quarter. This comprised 19,000 broadband internet units, 15,000 fixed-line telephony and 4,000 video subscribers.

“I think there are some homes that we will not rebuild back to, and it’s just gone. For the most part, we think we can get back to a pretty high level of penetration,” Nair noted as the company brought 48,000 RGUs back online during the first six months of 2026.

Liberty’s Jamaican operation, led by Flow Jamaica, reported a US$5.2 million or two per cent reduction in six-month revenue to US$204.8 million.

The hurricane had a US$20 million negative impact to Liberty’s revenue and a US$22 million impact on its operating income before depreciation and amortisation.

Nair credited the recovery trajectory to the work of the company’s teams in Jamaica and Miami, including the managers overseeing its Jamaica operations.

Despite the headwinds it experienced from Hurricane Melissa, Flow Jamaica continues to expand its offerings to the Jamaican market. Flow launched the 5G network on June 11 providing coverage to approximately 70 per cent of Jamaica’s population. This service is available to residential and enterprise postpaid subscribers.

Flow also launched the ‘Unbeatable’ Network campaign as it pushes fixed mobile convergence which bundles fixed and mobile services. The fixed broadband service is backed by the ability to switch from home Wi-Fi to the mobile network during power outages. Mobile connectivity is, in turn, supported by satellite through Flow’s Starlink DTC partnership.

“The Unbeatable campaign is now live in Jamaica and Cayman and coming soon to other Liberty Caribbean markets, as well as being deployed across the broader LLA group. In the Caribbean, it encompasses the unique concept of an always-on network, both in fixed and mobile,” Nair said during his presentation.

The Category 5 hurricane and the recent El Niño phenomenon prompted analyst Matthew Harrigan to ask about the availability of parametric insurance in the Caribbean.

LILA Chief Financial Officer Chris Noyes said the company had parametric insurance coverage for the hurricane season.

Parametric insurance has helped Jamaica rebuild and recover from the last two major hurricanes, with a US$81-million payment from weather derivatives received in 2025.

“I think we are one of the key global issuers of the parametric. We were able to do it even with the event we had in Jamaica, with a very cost-effective cover similar to prior years,” Noyes told Harrigan.

Nair said the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) website has become a permanent monitoring tool for his team since July.

He added that LILA’s leadership team would visit NOAA’s headquarters in Boulder, Colorado, to meet climatologists and hurricane experts.

LILA’s consolidated revenue increased one per cent to US$1.10 billion for the second quarter, US$10 million above analysts’ estimates.

Due to lower impairment and restructuring charges, LILA reported an operating profit of US$181.2 million compared to an operating loss of US$333 million. LILA’s adjusted OIBDA grew five per cent to US$436 million.

With a 34 per cent reduction in non-operating expenses to US$157.2 million, LILA reported a profit before tax of US$24 million versus a loss before tax of US$570.8 million.

However, higher taxes resulted in LILA reporting a consolidated net loss of US$10.6 million, with a US$24-million loss attributable to shareholders.

LILA’s consolidated revenue for the six-month period edged up to US$2.19 billion, while the company reported an operating profit of US$326.4 million, compared with an operating loss of US$204.9 million.

The net loss attributable to shareholders improved to US$46.7 million from US$559.7 million.

LILA’s asset base stood at US$12.23 billion, including US$3.78 billion in property and equipment and US$714.1 million in cash. Total liabilities stood at US$11.23 billion, while equity attributable to shareholders was US$528.1 million.

LILA’s Class C shares traded at US$8.54 on Thursday, while its Class A shares traded at US$8.66. The company has repurchased US$60 million of its common shares and has US$140 million remaining under its share-repurchase programme.

“As we look to [the] rest of 2026, we intend to build upon our H1 operational progress and lap the October 2025 Jamaica hurricane, all of which should set us up for a strong fourth quarter and positive momentum leading into 2027,” Nair said.

World.title: Germany’s gas gamble puts Europe’s winter at risk
World.content:
The low reserves have already added to the increased pressure on gas prices linked to renewed tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, with the European natural gas benchmark now consistently higher than it was for the first four months of the Iran war.

The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, has said the bloc faces no winter supply risks. But a report by energy analytics firm Rapidan projects that reserves will rise to only 65 percent of total storage capacity by November, arguing that hitting the EU's target by winter won't be possible without "materially higher prices."

That risk has been exacerbated, analysts say, by the bloc’s move in recent years to replace its long-term supply deals with Russia with short-term purchases of globally traded liquefied natural gas. These seaborne cargoes are highly mobile and go to the highest bidder — leaving buyers more exposed to volatility on international markets, especially in the wake of the loss of key supplies from Qatar and rising demand in Asia.

A tanker passes through the Strait of Hormuz on Feb. 25, 2026. | Fadel Senna/AFP via Getty Images

Germany, the bloc's largest gas consumer, has seen its reserves fill up even more slowly than others, in part thanks to its more hands-off, market-led approach to restocking than many of its neighbors. As a result, reserves stood at only 47 percent of national capacity in August, according to the latest data — the lowest fill level since records began. That's especially worrying as the country's reserves are important for the bloc as a whole, representing over 20 percent of the EU's storage capacity.

Nevertheless, Berlin is staying the course. While its energy ministry has acknowledged the country's historically low reserves, it has refused to intervene to direct its main state-controlled gas buyers, SEFE and Uniper, to buy gas at current prices to ensure its targets are met, instead of waiting for market conditions to improve.

"It is the responsibility of companies and traders to fill the storage facilities for the winter," a spokesperson for the German energy ministry told POLITICO. "Government-led filling of the storage facilities would further constrain the gas market and drive prices even higher. The supply situation over the coming months would actually deteriorate."

World.title: Italy says it won’t take orders from Spain on border checks
World.content:
Earlier in the day, the Spanish government had threatened to take “proportional measures” if Rome did not stop its reintroduced border checks and temporary suspension of the Schengen Agreement by Aug. 9.

In its statement, Rome said it would keep these controls in place “at least until August 15 and, in any case, until security and terrorism risks to Italy can be completely ruled out,” adding that a new “migratory wave” is expected in Ceuta on that date.

“Only when it is certain that there will be no security or terrorism risks for Italy, that there will be no new wave and that there are no irregular migrants heading toward European territory will it be possible to reconsider what has already been decided,” said the document.

World.title: EU adds 5 people to Russia sanctions list after latest deadly attacks on Ukraine
World.content:
Russia this week carried out one of its deadliest barrages on Kyiv, killing 17.

The EU has added five individuals to its Russia sanctions list. The move was driven by Moscow’s “intensified strikes deliberately targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure” in Ukraine, according to a press release.

The press release does not refer to a specific attack, but earlier this week Russia carried out one of its deadliest barrages on the Ukrainian capital, killing 17. In July, a similar attack in Kyiv killed 12.

Among those included in the new sanctions is Ramil Badgutdinov — the head of a company that helps produce the Iskander-M ballistic missiles — and Aleksandr Dyukarev, head of the KrasMash plant that produces Sarmat ballistic missiles. Russia has not yet used Sarmat missiles in Ukraine, but Moscow has been testing them.

World.title: Madrid threatens retaliation if Italy keeps border controls on travelers from Spain
World.content:
In addition to slamming Rome for imposing border controls that inconvenienced thousands of passengers by creating legal uncertainty in the middle of the summer holiday season, Madrid also took Italy to task for criticizing Spain’s handling of migrants while failing to protect its own borders.

Even though “Italy is the EU member state that has recorded the highest number of irregular crossings in recent years, with figures that have at times been twice those of Spain … Spain has never introduced controls on travelers from Italy,” the Spanish government said.

Madrid has now given the Italian government two days to either lift the border controls or face reciprocal measures that aim to “protect the interests and dignity” of Spanish citizens.

“Governments should work to promote understanding between countries and serve the general interests of their populations, rather than create divisions and pointless conflicts driven by domestic electoral considerations,” the statement said.

“We trust that Europeanism, common sense and good faith will prevail.”

World.title: Musk says French Greens’ presidential candidate should be ‘shut down’
World.content:
“I’d rather be accused of defending democracy than of trying to buy it.”

Musk, who is a former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump, has regularly weighed in on European politics and thrown his support behind far-right candidates and parties — and France is no exception.

In July, Musk said far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen was “France’s last hope,” but her National Rally party was quick to downplay his backing to avoid being associated with the controversial owner of Tesla and SpaceX.

Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon also slammed Musk’s attacks against Tondelier on Thursday, before accusing the French government of not doing enough to fight foreign interference.

“The French presidential election is an open bar for all the manipulators in the world,” he wrote — a criticism Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot promptly rejected.

Earlier this week, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government was boosting efforts to detect and punish foreign interference in the upcoming 2027 election, while presidential candidates Gabriel Attal and Édouard Philippe, as well as likely candidate Raphaël Glucksmann shared they had been victims of Russian disinformation campaigns.

World.title: Week Ender: Verhofstadt on “Trumpism”, plus summer must-reads
World.content:
It’s August in Brussels, which means it’s vacation time.

Whether you’re heading off to the beach or holding down the fort in town, this episode is brimming with book recommendations from our newsroom and from you, our listeners. Whatever your genre preference, from true crime thrillers to deep political dives, we’ve got your summer holiday covered.

But this installment is not just a book chat.

We’re also tackling the rise of populism and the crises facing liberal democracies around the world. That’s the topic of “Defeating Trumpism,” a new book by former Belgian Prime Minister and European Parliament Member Guy Verhofstadt. World.title: Low Danube water reveals Wehrmacht motorbike on riverbed
World.content:
The water level in the Danube has never been this low. The low water has revealed what lay hidden on the riverbed for decades, among them a Wehrmacht motorcycle, a DKW NZ 350-1 model from the Second World War.

 

It was found in the riverbed in the heart of Hungary's capital, Budapest, at the level of the Hungarian parliament building. For staff at the local Institute and Museum of Military History it is a genuine once-in-a-century discovery. The vehicle is almost completely intact, according to the institute. It was preserved in the Danube's mud.

DKW racing motorcycles from 1939 and 1931, archive Copyright 2007 AP. All rights reserved.

The motorcycle recovered is a model that was developed specifically for wartime use and was produced from 1944 onwards. Around 12,000 units were built by the end of the war in 1945. Its predecessor, the DKW (source in German) NZ 350, reached a top speed of 105 km/h, according to the ADAC.

The motorcycle was manufactured by Auto Union AG, a car and motorcycle producer founded in 1932. Auto Union AG was created through the merger of several brands, including Audi.

By autumn 1936 the NZ range, made up of the 250 and 350 models, was ready for mass production. However, because another motorbike range was selling so well, they did not go into series production until 1938.

On earlier models from the manufacturer the frame sections were still bolted together. On the NZ range they were welded. Because this required a large amount of electricity, the work could only be carried out at night, when the power grid was not otherwise under heavy load.

German troops drive through Liège, 30 May 1940 AP

German anti-tank mines, remnants of hand grenades and artillery shells have also been found on the bed of the Danube. The Hungarian Institute of Military History says this stretch of the river may have been used as a "war rubble dump".

From March 1944 German troops besieged Budapest. Between October 1944 and February 1945 the Battle of Budapest took place between the Soviet Red Army and German and Hungarian forces. Around 30,000 German, more than 17,000 Hungarian and about 80,000 Soviet and Romanian soldiers were killed. After the surrender of the remaining German units, Budapest was liberated on 13 February 1945.

World.title: Russian attacks on Kyiv region kill three, including a child
World.content:
Three people, including a child, have died following Russian attacks on the Kyiv region overnight, according to local authorities.

 

Timur Tkachenko, the head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said Russian forces had struck three sites in the Brovary district near the capital, killing three people and injuring three others.

"Falling debris has damaged a private residential house, outbuildings and cars. A fire also broke out on the premises of a non-residential building," he wrote in a post on Telegram.

At least four people were also injured in an attack on the city of Kyiv, per the Kyiv City Military Administration.

Firefighters have been battling flames in the city's Holosiivskyi and Obolon districts, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) reported on social media, while sharing images showing blazes ravaging what appeared to be warehouses and garages.

A Russian drone strike on the Chernihiv region in northern Ukraine also sparked a fire at a warehouse in the Pryluky district, per the DSNS. No casualties have been reported so far.

Zelenskyy in Serbia

It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Serbia, where he is set to meet with Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić and Prime Minister Đuro Macut.

According to Zelenskyy, the trio are due to discuss "expanding economic ties" as well as their relationship with the European Union and security issues.

US Senate approves Russia sanctions bill

On Friday, the United States Senate passed a sweeping new round of sanctions on Russia.

The bill, which had been championed by the late Lindsey Graham, is designed to punish Moscow and countries that purchase its oil and natural gas.

Responding to the news on X, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was "very grateful" and that the sanctions package would help "increase pressure" on Moscow and bring this "insane Russian war against our independence and our people to an end."

"Real, strong American pressure and sanctions against Russia are what will help the most," he added.

World.title: Porto Santo travel guide: Escape to one of Europe’s most underrated islands
World.content:
There’s something wonderfully easy about arriving in Porto Santo.

 

Just a short flight or a two-and-a-half-hour ferry from Funchal, Madeira’s busy capital, the tiny Portuguese island feels a world away from the crowds and bustle of its larger neighbour, despite the two being just 81 kilometres apart.

Madeira has long been a favourite alternative to Spain's Canary Islands, drawing visitors with its dramatic landscapes, hiking trails and subtropical climate. Porto Santo, by comparison, has remained something of a secret.

That may well be set to change, though, after Expedia recently ranked it second in its annual Hot List of European islands to know now.

Porto Santo is pretty diminutive, even for an island. At just 11 kilometres across, it’s small enough to explore without ever feeling as though you need to be anywhere in particular.

That, really, is the appeal.

Rather than cramming your days with sightseeing or meticulously planning an itinerary, you can spend the morning wandering along the coast, stop for a long lunch and still have plenty of time left to find a quiet stretch of sand before sunset.

Head to the beach – and take a dip in the Atlantic

The beach – Praia do Porto Santo – is undoubtedly one of the island’s biggest draws and absolutely a must-see.

Saskia explored the small - but buzzy - island of Porto Santo via buggy Saskia O'Donoghue

It’s a vast sweep of golden sand that stretches for around nine kilometres along the southern coast – nearly the entire length of the island.

The sand is so deep, I felt myself sinking into it as I ran across it in the July heat for a much-needed, cooling dip in the Atlantic Ocean that surrounds the island.

That water is certainly inviting and, even in the height of summer, the beach must be one of quietest in Europe, possibly due to its sheer size. Whatever the reason, there’s a sense that you can find your own little corner of the island here – and relax in peace.

When I’d had enough beach time, it was time for adventure.

Explore the island via buggy

Enter: Porto Santo Buggy Adventures. Run by the charming Tiago, who knows the island inside out, it was a great way to see the sights, while off-roading on exciting terrains.

For someone used to driving a Fiat 500, with an embarrassingly low top speed, I was a little nervous about being put in sole charge of a buggy but, as I strapped on goggles to protect my eyes, I realised I needn’t have worried.

It was genuinely one of the most fun experiences of my life so far.

I’d booked a 90-minute tour, but the excursion ran for much longer, and I felt I’d checked off plenty of must-sees on the island.

First was the Flores viewpoint, where I marvelled over much of the island from above, as well as smaller islets, once used for limestone mining.

Next up, we headed to the Dunas de Porto Santo. The landscape feels surprisingly remote, almost otherworldly, with rolling dunes creating an almost desert-like environment.

The otherworldly Dunas de Porto Santo is best explored by buggy Saskia O'Donoghue

It’s made up of the finest of sand and fossils which combine to give the impression of being on the moon or another, unexplored planet – something that contrasts sharply with the sea just beyond.

Porto das Salemas was the next stop, a place where natural pools form among the rocks. At low tide, the water settles into clear, sheltered pools that are ideal for cooling off, particularly on a warm day.

I spotted colourful crabs in their natural habitat and chatted with families who bring picnics to the shore.

Stupidly, I’d forgotten to pack my swimsuit, but couldn’t resist a quick dip in my underwear. Usually, I’d be horribly embarrassed, but this island is so laid back, no one seemed to mind.

By the end of my buggy trip, my hair, skin and clothes were covered in Porto Santo’s notoriously intrusive fine dust but, truly, I was beaming as I hopped in the shower, high on adrenaline.

Clean again, it was time to eat.

Enjoy the local cuisine – and the relaxation

Of course, no trip to an island is complete without eating your way through the local specialities – and that’s certainly the case here.

One dish to look out for is scabbard fish, traditionally served with banana and passionfruit. It might sound like an unusual combination at first, but the sweet fruit works surprisingly well with the delicate fish.

Then there’s poncha, the island’s answer to a holiday cocktail. Made with sugar cane rum, citrus and sugar, it’s fresh and punchy, and best enjoyed slowly as the sun starts to disappear.

The pools of Porto das Salemas are a natural wonder on Porto Santo Saskia O'Donoghue

That’s perhaps the secret to Porto Santo. It’s not an island that demands much from you. There are no endless lists of attractions to tick off or packed schedules to follow.

For anyone looking to escape the crowds of better-known European beach destinations, it offers a quieter alternative without sacrificing the things that make an island holiday so appealing.

You get long beaches, warm seas, dramatic landscapes and excellent food, all within a place small enough to explore at your own pace.

Sometimes, the best holiday is the one where you have nowhere else to be – and Porto Santo is a perfect example of that.

Saskia O'Donoghue travelled to Porto Santo as a guest of Expedia.

A four-night stay in Porto Santo available to book on Expedia between 19-23 October 2026 starts at £642 (approx €749) per traveller including accommodation at Pestana Porto Santo Beach Resort & Spa and flights from London Heathrow via Lisbon to Porto Santo with TAP. Alternatively, you can bundle up the same accommodation with flights from Luton to Funchal with easyJet on Expedia from £465 per traveller and take a ferry from Funchal to Porto Santo. Ferry sold separately with Porto Santo Line.

World.title: Batteries can save Europe’s solar and wind power from being wasted. But are they a blackout risk?
World.content:
Batteries have been touted as a “crucial technology” in the EU’s clean energy transition, but have recently been hit with concerns over blackouts.

 

As the bloc’s share of renewable energy is estimated to reach around 69 per cent by 2030 and 80 per cent by 2050, the need for flexible storage is rapidly increasing.

Europe already wastes millions of euros worth of wind and solar energy due to grid constraints and their inflexible nature. When supply outstrips demand, this can trigger negative electricity prices.

Many experts have identified battery energy storage systems (BESS) as a silver-bullet solution to this issue. The logic is simple: batteries can store electricity produced by renewables during the day (when consumption tends to be low) and release it to households when demand increases in the evening.

It’s why Europe installed 36 GWh of new BESS in 2025, bringing total operational capacity beyond 100 GWh for the first time. This is enough to power roughly 75 million homes.

“Across Europe, battery storage is helping integrate growing volumes of renewable energy, strengthen energy security and improve power system resilience,” says trade association SolarPower Europe.

“As the continent seeks to reduce its dependence on costly fossil fuel imports, accelerate electrification and meet its climate goals, storage can no longer be viewed as a supporting technology. It is becoming a strategic asset, instrumental to strengthening Europe’s resilience, competitiveness and energy sovereignty.”

Has the battery boom gone too far?

Last week, British newspaper The Telegraph published an article headlined “Britain’s battery boom ‘risks overwhelming the grid’” – claiming that back-up systems supporting wind power could trigger “the blackouts they are trying to avoid”.

The article follows a recent report from the Panel of Technical Experts, an advisory group of independent consultants appointed by the UK government to advise on technical aspects of electricity market reform.

“The PTE continues to consider that some thought needs to be given to the way BESS is likely to behave in a Capacity Market Notice (CMNs) situation, as storage may then have an incentive to charge in advance to fulfil their CM obligations,” the report reads.

“This may result in a fast descent into a stress event. This additional demand may need to be more explicitly modelled when estimating the peak demand in a stress event.”

A CMN is a signal four hours in advance that there may be less energy generation available than system operators expect they will need to meet national demand.

However, the report is not saying that batteries will destabilise the grid and does not explicitly express concern over blackouts. Instead, it is simply highlighting the need for modelling on how batteries react to a CMN.

Is Europe’s battery boom risking blackouts?

Fears that batteries could trigger blackouts across Europe mainly revolve around the fact that grid operators cannot see and cannot control lots of small, distributed installations.

It means if they all operate in unison, it would be difficult to manage.

“This is the same challenge we have been managing with solar power for the last 20 years,” Adrian Hiel, director of the Electrification Alliance tells Euronews Earth.

“We have steadily gotten better and better at ensuring that [installations] improve the grid rather than harm it. Realistically this only becomes a blackout risk if we ignore the fact that we are installing millions of batteries annually. No one is interested in doing that.”

The main solution for dealing with the “tiny risk” posed by batteries is better modelling, Hiel says. This will allow grid operators to anticipate how battery fleets behave in certain situations.

Batteries are going to be a much bigger help to the grid than hindrance. Adrian Hiel Director of the Electrification Alliance

“We can expect relatively large margins of error in their modelling in the next couple of years but then the models will get more and more precise and accurate – just as they did with modelling how rooftop solar will behave,” he adds.

“The other solution for managing batteries on the grid will be aggregating control by a third party. So instead of a household managing how their individual battery operates, a company will bring together tens or hundreds of thousands of batteries and run them for the maximum household value and the maximum grid benefit.”

This idea is already being rolled out with smart electric vehicle (EV) charging in many countries. Hiel describes it as a “logical next step” for batteries too – as it means that a grid operator can contact the battery aggregator to either start consuming quickly, by charging, or start discharging quickly to meet sudden demand increases.

Are batteries really ‘very expensive’?

An industry voice quoted in the article also claims that “batteries are very expensive” but no data is provided to back this up. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), average battery costs have plummeted by 90 per cent since 2010 due to advances in chemistry and manufacturing.

A recent report from energy think-tank Ember found that by 2030, utility-scale batteries could deliver short-term flexibility in the EU at 20 per cent lower cost than new gas plants.

It also found that in the next four years, EU batteries could deliver in a single hour more than 80 per cent of the power that all EU gas power plants combined can generate in the same period.

Graph showing that batteries can deliver short-term flexibility in the EU at cheaper costs than new gas plants Ember

“Clean flexibility is here,” says Beatrice Petrovich, a senior energy analyst at Ember.

“Rapid growth in batteries, EV smart charging and heat pumps can reduce reliance on gas for grid balancing and ease grid strain. The task now is not innovation but execution: remove barriers, reward flexibility and scale these solutions fast enough to avoid locking in unnecessary fossil backup.”

Should Europe just go back to fossil fuels?

The Telegraph interviewee suggests that potential cost barriers and blackout risks mean that countries should halt the clean energy transition and keep their reliance on fossil fuels.

“Claiming that we shouldn’t build intermittent generation because of this tiny risk from batteries is a bit like telling a morbidly obese person that they shouldn’t lose weight because they will have to buy new clothes,” Hiel says.

“The inconvenience of managing the impact of these millions of batteries is infinitesimally small compared to the benefits of maximising the cheapest sources of energy the world has ever known at a time when the countries who sell us gas talk about dominating Europe energetically and threaten to withhold that gas if we don’t do as they say.”

The UK’s Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) refused to comment when asked whether it was concerned about blackouts from the battery boom. It did not answer any questions asked by Euronews Earth – providing the same quote it gave to The Telegraph.

“Our capacity market ensures security of supply while providing value for money for consumers,” a spokesperson said. “We’ve cut VAT on electricity to give families breathing space and our focus is working to bring bills down for good.”

World.title: Amanda Knox takes her story to the Edinburgh Fringe reigniting old wounds
World.content:
Nearly two decades after the murder of British student Meredith Kercher, Amanda Knox is once again at the centre of public attention. This time it is not because of a court case, but because of a comedy show she is performing at the Edinburgh Fringe.

 

The murder that made headlines

Kercher, a 21-year-old Leeds University student, was found stabbed to death on 2 November 2007 in the apartment she shared with Knox in Perugia, Italy. She had also been sexually assaulted.

The investigation quickly turned to Knox, then a 20-year-old American exchange student, and to Italian student Raffaele Sollecito, her boyfriend of only a few days. Both were arrested and convicted of murder and sexual assault, and spent years fighting the charges.

Amanda Knox poses for a portrait to promote "The Twisted Tale of Amanda Knox" 2025 Invision

Knox served nearly four years in prison before an appeal court freed her in 2011. After several further legal reversals, Italy's highest court definitively acquitted both Knox and Sollecito in 2015, ruling there was insufficient evidence to convict them.

A third man, Ivorian national Rudy Guede, was convicted of Kercher's murder in 2009 and sentenced to 30 years, later reduced to 16. He was released in 2021 after serving 13 years and has always denied killing her.

Since returning to the United States, Knox has rebuilt her public life as an author, podcaster and campaigner for people she says have been wrongly convicted. She published the memoir Free: My Search for Meaning in 2025.

From prison to the Fringe stage

Knox, now 39, is making her Fringe debut with Cartwheel, a one-woman comedy show running for 11 nights at the Gilded Balloon. The title refers to a long-circulated media claim that she turned cartwheels at a police station shortly after Kercher's death — an allegation that became part of the public image built around her during the investigation. The run has sold out.

Knox says the show explores what it is like to become one of the world's most vilified women, and the challenge of explaining that history to her young daughter.

"I talk about all of my experiences going through being vilified, but I also talk about the experience of trying to explain that to my daughter and how absurd that can be. Like telling my four-year-old daughter a Dr. Seuss fairy tale version of this very dramatic and serious thing that happened to me and people that I cared about."

The Kercher family's objections

The show has drawn a strong backlash from Meredith Kercher's family, who argue that a case involving such a violent crime is not appropriate material for comedy. Her sister, Stephanie Kercher, has said the production normalises and trivialises violence against women.

"We felt very strongly that the violence surrounding the theme is not appropriate for a platform at a comedy show. But I would have hoped that two decades on we'd maybe have a little bit more empathy around using this theme and association in such a traumatic event in our lives. I would really hope that moving forward, she can try to move away from Meredith's name. I very much understand that she has her own story to tell, but we've heard it many, many times now."

An online petition calling for the show to be cancelled, started by a family friend and backed by Stephanie Kercher, has gathered thousands of signatures. It argues that Cartwheel mocks the events surrounding the murder and turns a tragedy into entertainment.

Knox's response

Knox says she was not surprised by the criticism. "I can't say that I was anticipating a petition, but I was anticipating criticism and pushback, in the sense that I have always received criticism and pushback no matter what I've done."

She has also rejected the idea that mentioning the case inevitably harms Kercher's family. "I can't speak to what is or is not triggering to Meredith's family. What I can say is that I've never seen the kind of scrutiny and criticism pointed towards a wrongly accused man that I have seen pointed towards me."

Responding to the petition, Knox said the show honours Kercher's memory and confronts the violence done to her, and argued that calling for the cancellation of a production nobody has yet seen is not an argument against it.

Nearly two decades on, the case remains one of the most famous criminal investigations of the century. Knox's acquittal ended the legal battle, but her return to the spotlight has reopened a public debate over memory, justice and where the line falls between telling one's own story and revisiting a tragedy that still affects the victim's family.

World.title: US appeals court orders halt to Trump ballroom construction without congressional approval
World.content:
A federal appeals court has ordered the Trump administration to halt all construction of its $400 million White House ballroom until it receives congressional approval.

 

The US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit had initially allowed construction to continue while it considered the case, but then agreed with a lower court that such a massive White House overhaul required the explicit consent of Congress.

In a 2-1 decision on the ballroom, the appeals court sided with historic preservationists who sued to stop construction of the massive structure, which has begun to rise aboveground on the east side of the White House, according to the most recent aerial photos of the site.

The 8,400-square-metre ballroom is being constructed where the White House’s historic East Wing stood before Trump ordered its demolition last fall.

Construction continues on the White House ballroom, Friday, Aug. 7, 2026, in Washington. AP Photo/Allison Robbert

“Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” the court wrote.

“This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy. This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom.

“What it does mean,” the court continued, “is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorisation, as the Constitution and laws require.”

The court said it would stay its ruling for two weeks to give the administration time to appeal to the US Supreme Court.

US President Donald Trump lashed out after the ruling, calling it "horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful", and vowed to appeal the decision.

President Donald Trump tours Ballroom construction around the outside the White House, Tuesday, May 19, 2026, in Washington. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin

The two judges in the majority were appointed by Democratic presidents, while the dissenter was nominated by Trump himself.

Trump, who has repeatedly complained that the White House lacks sufficient space for grand galas such as state dinners, unilaterally ordered construction of the massive ballroom.

Trump has insisted that the ballroom will be privately financed, but media reports in June showed that significant taxpayer funds were going to the project

Democrats warned that $350 million in funds from a tax cuts law appeared to have been redirected for the ballroom.

Several of Trump's construction projects, including a proposed 76-metre-tall triumphal arch, have similarly faced legal challenges, but the ballroom project would be the first to reach the Supreme Court.

World.title: US Senate approves sweeping Russia sanctions bill targeting energy income
World.content:
The US Senate has overwhelmingly approved a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russia's energy revenues, including Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and the so-called shadow fleet.

 

The bipartisan legislation, which passed the Senate 86-11, would allow US President Donald Trump to set tariffs of up to 500% on Russian imports, including gas and oil.

It would also penalise countries that continue to buy Russian oil, gas and other exports, allowing Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including countries such as China and India.

US sanctions would also expand to target older, reflagged oil tankers that Russia uses to circumvent existing US sanctions on Russian oil and energy revenues.

The legislation now heads to the House of Representatives, though a vote there will not take place until at least early September due to the congressional summer recess.

If adopted into law, Putin himself would be among those targeted by the sanctions, as well as other top officials.

The negotiated bill also includes waiver authority for the president, allowing the White House to waive sanctions or restrictions if the president certifies to Congress that the waiver is in the national interest.

The show of force from the Senate is the most substantial move yet during Trump’s second term to shift the dynamic of the more than four-year war. Congress has struggled to ensure US funding and munitions flows to Ukraine, but Trump has given a nod to the sanctions package, putting pressure for the House to take it up for a vote and send it to the White House for his signature.

The bill was named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, who died on 11 July after spending more than a year building support for it.

Shortly before his death, Graham announced he had reached an agreement with the White House on a revised version of the text, including the extension of existing sanctions authority aimed at restricting funding for Iran's energy and weapons sectors.

World.title: The great Infantino divide: Who is for and against the controversial FIFA chief?
World.content:
As the 2026 World Cup drew to a close last month, many would have expected tournament organiser FIFA to slip back behind the scenes as fans around the world turned their attentions to their respective club teams once again.

 

FIFA, it seems, had other ideas.

The football world governing body sparked huge backlash in late July when it announced a plan to invite private investors to take stakes in a new subsidiary known as the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which would have run its commercial operations and events, including the World Cup.

The proposal, which FIFA said could raise up to $4.2 billion based on an initial valuation of $20 billion, prompted fierce criticism from across the football community.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino and his team have since scrapped the plan and issued an apology for the way the situation was handled, with Infantino vowing to fight on in his role despite mounting calls for him to step down.

The crisis has now evolved into a widening divide between confederations and associations across the globe.

Euronews has taken a look at who is getting behind the embattled FIFA chief and who is calling for change.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino, right, and Arsene Wenger, Chief Officer (FIFA) and former soccer coach arrive for the Women's Euro 2025 quarterfinals soccer match. Copyright 2025 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Against

European governing body UEFA has dished out particularly strong criticism of Infantino and the FFE idea, announcing that its 55 member associations would boycott FIFA competitions unless the plan was abandoned.

UEFA later said that FIFA's continued support for Infantino - who had already been facing scrutiny over his relationship with US President Donald Trump - and its apology over the FFE proposal "changes nothing."

"UEFA’s associations were very clear about the conditions attached to the non-participation in FIFA competitions," it said in a statement on Thursday. "First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn, and secondly, assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again," it said. "These conditions have not been met."

Some individual associations also moved quickly to withdraw support for Infantino's re-election bid as the controversy gathered pace.

Wales, Finland, Serbia, and Sweden were among the first to announce they would no longer back the FIFA president for another term, with the Serbian FA calling its decision the "only logical and rational course of action" after recent events had "seriously damaged the standing and reputation of both FIFA and its president."

They have since been followed by football associations from England, Norway, Jordan, and Albania.

The Norwegian FA went a step further, calling for Infantino to resign after it said its "trust" had been broken.

"We believe that trust has now been lost and that FIFA needs new leadership," Lise Klaveness, its president, said. "When trust is lost, the leadership must also be reassessed. We therefore believe that Gianni Infantino’s time as FIFA President should be over, and we are asking him to step down."

Spain players, from left, cheer alongside President Donald Trump and FIFA President Gianni Infantino at the conclusion of the World Cup. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

For

However, Infantino still retains some allies across the football world, in particular among associations working with smaller budgets, where ensuring continued funding is critical to remaining competitive.

On Thursday, the Confederation of African Football announced it had "unanimously reconfirmed its support" for Infantino while thanking him for his help developing African football.

"CAF will continue to focus on making African Football amongst the best in the world and is reaffirming its commitment to adhering to global governance, transparency and auditing best practices," its president, Patrice Motsepe, said.

In October, Infantino told an audience in Kinshasa that FIFA had invested more than $1 billion into African football through its FIFA Forward Programme since 2016. The Forward Programme helps provide development funding and support to FIFA's 211 member associations.

The governing body says it will have provided around $1.28 billion in support to the continent by the end of 2026.

World Cup cohosts Mexico are also standing behind Infantino, as are Paraguay and World Cup runners-up Argentina.

Despite heavy criticism of FIFA from the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football, of which it is a member, the Mexican Football Federation said it "supports president Infantino's leadership to continue driving the development of football through institutional strengthening."

For its part, Argentina, whose national team have been dealing with their own fair share of controversy in recent weeks, praised Infantino for his work since he was first elected as president in 2016 and commended him for recognising his "mistakes."

World.title: Typhoon Dolphin hits Japan as China braces for coming storm
World.content:
A typhoon is lashing Japan's south, causing injuries and blackouts. It is now headed for China, where ports have been closed in preparation.

Typhoon Dolphin raged over Japan's southern regions on Saturday, causing some injuries and blackouts.

Okinawa and Amami island in Kagoshima prefecture were the areas expected to be worst affected.

The storm is expected to move on to China, making landfall along its eastern and southern ‌coast between late Sunday and early Monday, with Chinese authorities shutting down ports and ferry services ahead of the storm.

What do we know about Typhoon Dolphin in Japan?

The typhoon has brought maximum sustained winds of 162 kilometers per hour (roughly 100 miles per hour) and ​gusts reaching ‌216 kph

Authorities in Okinawa prefecture said 240 people had taken shelter at evacuation centers in the region on Friday

Five elderly people were reported to have suffered non-life-threatening injuries

Japan Meteorological Agency forecast strong winds, heavy rain and high waves in the Okinawa region through Sunday

The Naha Airport on Okinawa Island said it closed on Friday, and all domestic and international flights in and out of Naha, the prefectural capital, have been canceled

Power was cut to some 14,000 buildings in Okinawa

What preparations is China making for Typhoon Dolphin?

The China National Meteorological Centre Typhoon Dolphin has said Typhoon Dolphin will probably make landfall between the city of Zhoushan in Zhejiang province and the city of Fuding in Fujian province.

Zhejiang has raised its coastal typhoon alert to its highest level, while ceasing port operations and suspending 162 passenger ferry routes.

The storm is expected to bring rain and strong winds to eastern China, including parts of Shanghai, through August 12.

Some parts of eastern Zhejiang could be in for a deluge, forecasters say, with more than 600 mm (23.6 inches) of rain possible.

Ningbo ⁠Lishe ​International Airport in Zhejiang said it will stop its operations from 11:30 ​p.m. (1530 GMT) on Saturday and suspend all flights on Sunday.

Fishing boats in Wenling in Zhejiang province have sought shelter ahead of the storm Image: Zhou Xuejun/Xinhua/AP Photo/picture alliance

Taiwan-China tensions over typhoon restrictions

Taiwan, where 63 international flights have been cancelled, is also expected to experience heavy rain in the north over the weekend.

New political friction between Taiwan and China has also arisen after Beijing ordered that ships passing through ⁠the Taiwan Strait must heed ​its traffic control

instructions amid the typhoon.

Taipei has slammed Beijing's injunctions as "ridiculous," saying that Beijing has no right to restrict access to international waters.

"The unreasonable and crude statement ‌by ​the relevant Chinese Communist departments reflects an ignorance, disregard, and trampling of international order and norms. It is utterly ridiculous!" Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council said in a statement late ​on Friday.

China regards the democratically governed island as a breakaway territory of its own and also claims to own the strategic strait, a stance rejected by both Taipei and Washington.

Edited by: Rana Taha
